speechtext:
I rise to a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. I read in ' La Pa trie ' of yesterday, in the parliamentary l.etter, the following paragraph :
Quelqu'un qui se croit au. fait des allees et venues politiquoe, m'assurait tout k l'heure que Particle trSs blessant publiS dans le " News," a etd inspird par sir Wilfrid Laurier lui-meme.
Which I will translate as follows :
Some body who thinks that he knows what is going on in the political world assured me a moment ago that the most offensive article published in the * News ' has been inspired by Sir Wilfrid Laurier himself.
This matter came up incidentally yesterday, and I have only to say again that there is no foundation at all for this statement. Neither directly nor indirectly, in any shape or form, did I inspire that article. I never knew of its publication until my attention was called to it yesterday at three o'clock.

BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Before the Orders of the Day are called. I again press upon the attention of the Prime Minister, and upon the attention of the government, the extreme desirability of having their railway policy immediately brought down if w-e are going to have a railway policy brought down during the present session. Yesterday I asked my right hon. friend to give us some information as to the date. I asked him in the first place whether or not we are to have that policy during the present session ; and, in the second place, if we are going to have it during the present session, at what date may we expect it. It is perhaps only right to again remind the government that we have entered upon the fifth month of the session. In the expectation of all of us when we came here, the government measures would have been down two months ago, and had that been the case, we would have been very much further on with our work than we are at present. It is not to be expected that an important measure of that kind is to be brought down after the estimates are all passed and in the closing days of the session. My right hon. friend himself would not regard that as a proper course of conduct. Indeed, in the days gone by, his voice, and the voice of many hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, was raised in strong protest against the bringing down of railway subsidies in the closing days of the session. This is an infinitely more important matter than any of these subsidies which excited criticism in times past, and yet we are nearing what ought to be the close of the session, and we have not an intimation even from the government as to the date when their policy will be brought down. In all fairness to the House and to the country, my right hon. friend ought to tell us whether or not we are to expect that policy, and if we are to expect it during this session he should give some definite and specific assurance as to the date within which we may expect it to be submitted to the House.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The request which niy hon. friend makes is not at all unreasonable, and I am quite willing to give him all the information which it is in my power to give him at this moment. I expect that we may be able to bring down a resolution with regard to the railway policy of the government some time next week, and perhaps early next week. I hope that we shall be able to take up the subject for discussion, perhaps not next week, but, if agreeable to my hon. friend, the early part of the week following ; because I suppose that when my hon. friend sees the resolution he would require some days before being prepared to take up the subject for discussion. Without binding myself absolutely ; if my hon. friend will renew his question on Monday or Tuesday next, perhaps I would he able then to give him an absolutely definite answer.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: 1 may assure my right hon. friend that I shall certainly renew my question if he does not bring down the policy within a very short period ; and I am afraid I shall have to comment on the delay in that case a little more at length than I have done to-day.

Bill (No. 223) to amend the Act of 1S99, respecting the city of Ottawa, read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
The MINISTER OB'1 FINANCE. I may say that this Bill is entirely a transcript of the resolutions with which the House has already dealt. There is no new matter whatever in it.
On section 2,
What is the security for that ?
The grants made by the government of Canada from time to time will be the source from which both the interest and the principal will be paid, under the security of this Act.
I understand that we give them $60,000 per annum, which they will have the right to spend, and they will have the right to borrow $250,000 more. ,

No, my hon. friend is mistaken. Out of the annual grant of $60,000 the commission will have to provide for everything. There is no increase in the amount of the grant, and no obligation beyond the amount of the grant.

It seems to me that this is the commencement of a system which is very like the grants to the Montreal Har-

bour Commission, to be added to from time to time, and that this whole grant will be taken up in the payment of interest, while in the end the Dominion will have to shoulder the debt and relieve the city of the expense.

After the commission have reserved out of the annual grant a sufficient sum to pay the interest and the instalments of principal, there will be left a very considerable sum of money, quite enough to enable them to meet all the expenses of maintenance. There is not the least danger of the Dominion being called upon to pay any of this debt otherwise than by the annual grant.
That is the usual history of these cases, and I have no doubt it will be the same with this.
I would remind my hon. friend that we have improved.

The hon. minister, in'introducing the resolutions did not give any explanation as to what induced the government to continue this grant for a further period of ten years. My recollection is that he merely said that the government had arrived at the conclusion that whoever was in power at the end of ten years would do this, and therefore that we might as well do it now. Is it in the contemplation of the government to continue the grant indefinitely and make it a perpetual grant, or has that been considered ?

My hon. friend is very kind in assuming that at the the end of this further period of ten' years we shall still be in office ; but I would not like to bank too much on that. Therefore, I would not like to say what will be the policy of the government some sixteen years from the present time. I do not think we ought to be so presumptuous as to say what shall be the policy of the- government sixteen years hence. Accidents might happen; though it is not likely, some of us might be out of office at that time. But, to be serious, the view we take is that by giving the commission this power now, they will be able to do things on a larger scale than they could do otherwise. They will be able to acquire land, and work out a larger and more comprehensive scheme of beautifying tfie city of Ottawa than they could if we confined them to the annual grant, out of which they could not make any considerable land purchases or carry out any very extensive scheme.
The same thing might be accomplished by increasing the amount and limiting the time. The policy seems to be to give them this grant for twenty years and to do nothing further.
Yes, we take authority to say what they shall do.

I mean nothing further as to the continuance of the grant. As to the hon. gentleman being in power at the end of sixteen years, it is quite possible that that may be the case ; but it will be after a vacation of fifteen years, if we can judge the present indications at ail correctly. My hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) suggests after a prolonged period of rest. I would be inclined to add another adjective, and say after a prolonged and enforced period of rest.

Still, my hon. friend does justice to us to this extent, that he believes that, after a period of vacation, our record will be so good that the country will be only too glad for us to come back to offiee after its experience of lion, gentlemen opposite.
No, but because after a period of sixteen years the country will have forgotten the hon. gentleman's misdeeds.
Over what term does the original grant extend ?
The original grant was for ten years, of which four years have now elapsed. We are extending it for another ten years, or sixteen years from the present time.

In view of the fact that the duties of the commissioners have been somewhat increased, that the grant of $60,000 is to be extended for a further period of ten years, and that the city is in reality contributing one-fourth of this amount, I think now is the proper time to suggest that the city should have another representative on the board. The city has only one representative on the board at present. I do not think it would be asking too much of the government to ask them to add the city engineer or the chairman of the board of works or some other representative of the city to the board in addition to the mayor.

If this were a joint fund, contributed to by the Dominion and by the city for some joint object, there would be force in my hon. friend's argument; but inasmuch as the whole benefit of this fund will go to the city of Ottawa, I do not think my hon. friend is likely to make a case that the interest of the city of Ottawa suffers. In whatever way this money is expended, it is primarily for the benefit of the city of Ottawa. Therefore it is not a case of ordinary partnership. It is a case where all the benefit goes to one of the parties.

I can hardly agree with the hon. Minister of Finance in that. He must be aware that for many years the government paid $15,000 to the city ; so that to-day the city is contributing at least one-fourth of the $60,000. I think the gov-

eminent gets good value for the money. I do not see why Ottawa should not have an additional representative on the commission.

Besides the mayor of Ottawa, the commission is composed of Mr. Bate, chairman, Messieurs Jos. Riopelle, C. R. Cunningham and George O'Keefe, all leading citizens of Ottawa ; and last session three other gentlemen, Sir William Kingston, Senator Casgrain and Senator Frost were added to the commission. It must he admitted therefore that the $15,000 contribution of the city is well looked after by these five Ottawa gentlemen, including the mayor. In fact the administration of the whole work is largely in the hands of these gentlemen.
Those gentlemen are, however, not responsible to the city for the expenditure of the $15,000 yearly, but only to the Dominion government.
Every one of these Ottawa gentlemen is a large ratepayer and influential citizen, and in that respect responsible to the city, and the mayor is besides responsible in his official capacity.
Could the city of Ottawa remove them if it wished ?

No, of course not, because they are appointed by the government just as the mayor is. The mayor is appointed under the Bill and not by the city. The Bill provides that the mayor shall be exofficio a member of the commission, but he is appointed by grace of parliament and not by the city.
I do not agree with my hon. friend in his contention that the mayor has not any right to sit.
I did not say anything of the kind. I would not say anything so nonsensical.
As I understood the Minister of Finance the other day, in introducing his resolutions, this money is to be capitalized for the purpose of adding to the Rockliffe Park?
Yes.

And that he had options from Mr. Keefer and several other proprietors in that vicinity. Has he any objection to let us know what the options are. so that we may realize at once whether he is making proper investment or not. Let me draw the hon. gentleman's attention to another thing. There is a park north of the railway station, which is in a dilapidated and disgraceful state. There is another field near Sandy Hill, which was formerly a cemetery and from which sand is now being carted. The bones of the dead are exposed and it is in a most disgraceful condition, especially when we consider that it is right in the centre of the capital of the
Dominion. In view of the fact that the government is contributing largely towards the beautifying of the city, it should insist that this field be taken care of. It might be made a beautiful portion of the city, and as we are spending a good deal on these improvements, our wishes should to some extent be consulted by the commission and the civic authorities.

The commission will be glad to receive the suggestions of my hon. friend. My hon. frieml was slightly inaccurate in saying that we had options on certain properties. The go-ernment have no options, but I understand that the commission have received some.
I have been told the amount but have forgotten what it is. I have no reason to doubt, from information that has reached me, that the options are fair and reasonable, but I have advised the commissioners to take the precaution of appointing valuators, so that parliament will be fully satisfied. With regard to the parks, the city makes an annual grant to its own park committee for the maintenance of parks and some of these places to wuich my hon. friend refers. I quite agree that all these parks should be improved, and have no doubt that the commission and the civic committee will co-operate and lose no effort to carry out the suggestions of my hon. friend.
I have every reason to believe that the cemetery lands were originally ordinance lands and, therefore, came under the Interior Department.

If that be the case, an arrangement could be made between the Department of the Interior and the commission for the improvement of this field, and no doubt the commission will be glad to take notice of the suggestion of my hon. friends and will endeavour to meet their wishes.

We are all interested in this work as well as the citizens of Ottawa. In my opinion, it requires as competent an engineer to look after this work as is required for the city of Ottawa. I am informed that the gentleman who fills the position is not competent. At least he was not found competent while in the employ of the city of Ottawa. If hon. members of this House will take an hour some day and go through some of the streets which have been improved by this engineer, I have no doubt that they will come to the conclusion, if they have any experience, that these streets are not properly completed. Some steps should be taken to have a competent engineer appointed.

This is the first intimation I have had of any doubt as to the competency of the engineer who is assisting the commission. I cannot undertake to give any judgment of my own.

because I have not tbe necessary knowledge. but tbe only impression I have received, from general observation, is that the work is very well done. However, I am not an engineer, and my opinion may not count for much. But the commissioners can have no Interest in appointing other than a competent officer, and I have no reason to doubt that if they found this man incompetent, they would appoint a competent man in his place.

I have conversed with very competent men In this city, who are capable of judging, and after carefully looking over the streets, they assured me that these streets are not 'properly completed and would have been much better done had a competent engineer been in charge.
By what authority is the mayor a member of the commission?
The original Act provides that the mayor shall be a member of the commission.

I ask that question because the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Bel-court) said that he was no more responsible to the city of Ottawa than any other member of the commission, but since the mayor is elected every year, the people have an opportunity of removing him, which they have not in the case of other members of the commission.

I did not say that the mayor is not responsible to the city of Ottawa, but that there is a distinction between the responsibility of the mayor to the city of Ottawa and the responsibility of the other members of the commission. I admitted there was a distinction. I pointed out that all the other gentlemen are responsible to the city, because they are influential and important ratepayers. Though their responsibility is not of an official character in so far as the city is concerned, such as that of tihe mayor, they are, by reason of their position as citizens, under great responsibility.

But that responsibility is simply nothing, because the city cannot remove them no matter how much displeased the citizens may be with their conduct. But, in the case of the mayor, they can replace him at the end of his term if they do not approve of what he has done.
None of these gentlemen stands in any representative capacity towards the citizens except the mayor, as I understand. And he is one of a commission of about seven, is it ?
Eight.

If it be a correct view of the matter that one-quarter of this sum is actually provided by the city, because formerly it received that amount Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
I from the government in lieu of water rates and something of that kind, it would seem to me that the city of Ottawa, or rather the municipality of Ottawa, for that word makes my meaning a little clearer, should be entitled to some larger representation upon the commission than it has at present. According to the proportion it contributes, the city should have at least two out of the commission of eight, whereas now it has only one. Of course I do not overlook the fact that my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) has brought to cur attention, that these other gentlemen are citizens of Ottawa. But they are responsible only to the government. There is no responsibility to the municipality of Ottawa on the part of any of them except the mayor ; indeed some of them are not residents of Ottawa at all, though I make no criticism on that point.

I think the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) will be probably satisfied if I assure him that I for one, have not heard any one complain that tlie city was not sufficiently represented on the c mmission at this moment. I do not believe that there is a demand to-day in the city that there should be a larger representation of the city on that board. I believe that the citizens of Ottawa, as a whole, are very well satisfied with everything the commission has done, and with the plans for the future, so far as they have been made public. And. as representing the citizens, I take this opportunity of expressing their gratitude for what this parliament has done for the improvement of the city.
On section 4,	,

I notice that when this Bill was under discussion before, some reference was made to the question of lumber piling in the city. I have not had an opportunity to read ' Hansard,' and so do not know what was said. But I would like to ask. as a matter of information, whether Hie government insist on having any voice in the management of the affairs of the city with regard to this and other matters affecting the government's interests. The government has so much property here that it seems to me only just that some understanding should be reached, on wise lines, and the government will not be doing their whole duty, now that we propose to assist in beautifying the city, if they allow a system to continue which, in all human probability will, sooner or latter, destroy the greater portion of the city, including the government property.

The discussion of the lumber piling question took place the other day, arising out of the debate on this Bill, but not relating to it. That is a matter of

municipal regulation with which the government have nothing to do. In this Bill, we deal only with public matters which have nothing to do with the lumber piling question. We do not by this measure undertake to displace the authority of the municipality in any way. There was some reference the other day to the Washington system, which, undoubtedly, has some merits. Washington is governed by the national government, which contributes one-half the revenues of the city, the residents contributing the other half. There is much to be said in favour of that system. But there is this difference between the two cities, that Washington is almost entirely a residential city while Ottawa is a manufacturing and industrial city, and, with its great water-powers must always be so ; and so the system will not apply to it so easily as it would to a residential city. I like the Washington idea and would be glad if we could expand this gradually and have a district of Ottawa, a national district, governed entirely under the direction of this parliament. There would be advantages in that system but I rather think the citizens of Ottawa are hardly ready for it at present. They might not view with favour any attempt to bring in such a system, even if we had power to establish it. It would be a matter of provincial and not Dominion legislation. It may be that there will grow out of this some system of that character, but, at present I do not see how we can go beyond the work of the commission and dealing with the particular class of Improvements for which this aid is granted.

It seems to me it would be the simplest thing in the world. We propose to give through these commissioners, a certain sum of money. In making that gift we can tack on any conditions we please. One of those conditions might well be that the city should rid itself of a great danger which exists at the present time and which must continue to exist unless the city acts. We can do that without impropriety and without adopting the Washington system. We are the givers, and can make what conditions we please.

But our interest as a parliament and government is not greater than the interests of the individual citizen of Ottawa ; and surely we must trust the citizens of Ottawa, who have their own interests, their own rights, and their own property to protect. Surely we can trust them with what is after all a matter of municipal regulation. If these beautiful parliament buildings were burned down, great as the loss would be, the people of Canada are rich enough to provide another. But there are many citizens, who, if their houses were burned down are not rich enough to build new ones. Man for man, the interest of the citizens is greater than
ours, and I think we can trust them to regulate this matter.

Let that be granted, and the fact remains that we have greater power, and can exercise more control to make tiie city do what it should do, than any individual citizen whether rich or poor. ' We propose to give material assistance to the city and what we give belongs to the whole country. In making the gift we have the right to bring pressure to bear upon the council to do what they should do. We can make that a condition of this munificent gift. It is the proper thing to do, and the government has the power to do it.

Right and wrong are matters of opinion. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) speaks as if there were no difference of opinion on this subject. Yet. in this House the other day we had a clear difference of opinion expressed as to whether it was right or not to remove the lumber piles. I offered no opinion on that subject. But some citizens take one view and some another, and there is no absolute right or wrong in the matter.

I may say to the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) that the representatives of the city of Ottawa have that matter under consideration. If it is left to the council I feel sure they will deal with it in a manner satisfactory, not only to the citizens but to this parliament.
They are not making much headway, if we may judge by the papers.

You cannot always rely on what you see in the papers. The council represent the people, and the people can be depended upon to see that a proper settlement of this question is reached.

The Minister ot Finance and Receiver General shall hold, for the purpose of securing the repayment of deposits made in the government savings hanks and in the post office savings banks, an amount in gold or in gold and Canadian securities guaranteed by the government of the United Kingdom, equal to not less than ten per centum of the total amount of such deposits as such amount is ascertained from time to time.
Wheu were Canadian securities guaranteed by the government of the United Kingdom ?

That was done many years
6815.

ago, but of late years we bare not availed ourselves of it. We desired the endorsement of tbe imperial government many years ago for certain issues of securities when perhaps the credit of Canada was not as strong as it is now, and we gladly welcomed the greater security which came from endorsement by the imperial government. speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: I would ask the Minister of Finance if he has had any occasion to give his attention to an idea that has been prevalent for some time of founding in this country local co-operative banks such as they have established1 with great success in England, Germany, Italy, Austria, France, Belgium, and even in Russia, banks with small capital that can be established almost anywhere in a country place. I am not familiar with the details of the system. The idea has been thoroughly studied here by M. A. Desjardins, and I think in the town of Levis, in the province of Quebec, a bank of that description has been established by that gentleman, who is the chairman of that co-operative savings and loan association, w*hich I aim told, is a great success in every way. I do not know if the Minister of Finance or any one in his department has had occasion to study that system of banking and to ascertain whether it would be feasible to allow the establishment of these local banks under the protection of the law.

A short time ago my attention was directed to the subject by some members of this House, and also by a gentleman who is connected with the official staff of the House (Mr. Desjardins) and who is very familiar with the operations of the bank at Levis, and I believe has some connection with it. The system is a very interesting one indeed, and deserves study. I have given directions to have the matter inquired into and it may be that at another session we shall be able to give them some legal organization. For the present I cannot hold out the hope that we shall be able to do anything this session; but I can promise that during the recess the matter will be very carefully studied.

speechtext: It would be interesting to know what plan of survey and exploration is being pursued. In what direction are the officers going to operate this year ?

There are fifteen exploring parties now in the field; one in the Yukon, one in the Peace River district, one connected with the boundary survey north of the forty-ninth parallel in British Columbia, one in the anthracite region of the Rocky Mountains, one in the Keewatin district, three in northern Ontario, one in the Bay of Quinte district, one in the Lake St. John district, two in New Brunswick, two in Nova Scotia, and two whose locations are not yet definitely decided.

Could the hon. minister tell us who is going in the party to the Lake St. John district, and can he give us a little more precise information as to the direction that the exploration is going to take ? Is it to be due north of Lake St. John or to the east or to the west ?

I could not say. If my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) has any suggestion to make in connection with it I would be glad to consider it. The work has not progressed very far in so far as this season is concerned. ' The information comes from the director of the survey, and I am not quite familiar with the exact location or nature of the work they are doing.
Who is going to be in charge of the party ?
One of the technical officers. I cannot say which one.

Who is now at the head of the geological survey ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
Dr. Bell.

Does he hold a permanent appointment ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
No.

How long has he held a temporary appointment?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
Ever since the death of Dr. Dawson. .

Is there any reason why he should not be confirmed in his appointment ? I ask that because I know of him. I know that he has been a very long time employed by the department, and I believe has given great satisfaction. Is there any reason why the appointment should be only of a temporary character ?

The question which my hon. friend has asked is a somewhat delicate one. Dr. Bell has been in the service of the geological survey for some fourteen years. He was at once appointed to take charge of the work when Dr. Dawson died. All I care to say - at this moment is that I have not felt like recommending his permanent appointment up to the present time. I anticipate being able to make some changes which I have had in mind for the last two or three years in connection with the survey and possibly the permanent appointment of Dr. Bell, might be facilitated by these changes. What I propose to suggest is that that which may more properly be called economic work, or work directly connected with mining, shall be separate from the other work and that change I propose to carry out by means of legislation this session, and I was proposing an appropriation for that purpose which will account for the difference in the appropriation which is before us at the present time. I think the question of Dr. Bell's appointment can be settled if the plan is carried out, but lam not prepared to say any more at the present time. The discussion of the scientific qualifications of scientific men is rather a delicate subject and I hesitate to say any more about it.

I mentioned the matter because I have known Dr. Bell for a great many years and although not in a position to judge of his qualifications he appears to have the reputation of having fulfilled his duties properly.

I would not like to be understood as even remotely suggesting that Dr. Bell's qualifications, as far as scientific knowledge is concerned, are not sufficient, but in addition to scientific knowledge the management of the survey and the executive work connected with it have to be considered and the various qualifications that are necessary to carry it out successfully have to be taken into account. I will be responsible for the appointment when it is made, and I shall try to feel that I have discharged- that responsibility properly when I do make it. But in the meantime I do not care to say any more about it.
In what part of Nova Scotia is the geological party operating this season ?
I have not the exact location. The work of the parties is under the direction of Dr. Fletcher and they are now, I think, in the coal district.
They are in the county of Cumberland.

They have been in the eastern part of the province for several 214
years. I would like to have them visit the county I have the honour to represent, as it is supposed that there are in that county coal deposits of a very valuable character. We would like to ascertain positively whether such is the case or not, and if so would like to see these deposits of coal developed.

I did not hear my -hon. friend (Mr. Kaulbach) very well, but I understand him to suggest that it is desirable that some work should be done in the county of Lunenburg. I will be happy to note that and discuss it with my hon. friend.
air. KATJLBACH. My reason for making that request is in consequence of its being supposed there are deposits of coal in the county of Lunenburg and we are desirous of ascertaining whether there are or not, and if so, we would like to have that industry developed.

I have at various times discussed the work of the survey in Nova Scotia with members in the House from Nova Scotia aud have received suggestions from them and to the best of my ability I have endeavoured to carry them out. I am not familiar enough with the particular localities to be able to speak of them by name from recollection, but as far as possible I will endeavour to carry out the work that can be done. I will be very happy to consider my hon. friend's suggestion.

In reference to the director of the geological survey I understand that the hon. minister anticipates at an early day dividing the work of the department so as to constitute one section that will be more particularly devoted to work from an economic point of view and another which will be more purely scientific.
Yes, more purely scientific and largely topographical.

I would be very glad to contribute in any way towards the appointment of Dr. Bell on a permanent basis. I have had a good deal of interest always in watching the work of the geological survey and in reading the annual reports, and it seems to me that the work has been carried on very efficiently in that department since Dr. Bell has taken charge. I would be only too happy to learn that the changes contemplated by the minister will enable him to make a permanent appointment in that case.

I may say to the committee something that I will say at greater length, when I make the definite proposition I intend to make, that while I have no doubt of the great value of the work that has been done by the geological survey, the result of my ob-



serration and supervision of tlie work during the last seven years has led me to the conclusion that sufficient attention has not been given to making the results of the work of practical value, and easily available to the public. The difficulty is that information which has been collected at such a vast amount of expense to the country is not in a position to be availed of by tbe ordinary commercial man or the ordinary prospector. If, for instance, I were asked to furnish a person coming from a foreign country who desired to invest in Canada with the information available on the subject of iron in Canada, I would be utterly at a loss. All I would be able to do would be to refer him to the library of the geological survey. There is no place now in which such information is collected. My purpose in organizing a mining branch is primarily to bring about the result that we will have in succinct and in somewhat popular form, all the information of a practical and economic character made readily available and tbe first duty of the branch would be to put that in shape. During last year I gave some instructions that have been carried out pretty fully in respect to one particular subject, for instance, the subject of nickel. Dr. Barlow, a very capable officer, has been devoting himself last year to preparing a report on nickel. When that report is out I think we shall have all the information required with regard to nickel in Canada, so that any one who reads that book and understands it will know everything that is to be known about our nickel deposits. If any one asks for information with regard to the economic value of metals we ought to be able to give him that information in the best possible form. That is the principal fault I find with the survey as it is organized at the present time. Of course it is very difficult to make changes; everybody who is connected with an institutioh is inclined to think that that institution is managed on just about the proper line, but after six or seven years experience I am clear in my opinion that a change is not only desirable but necessary if the country is to get value for the work it is doing.

It seems to me that a very great deal of valuable work might be done at once by simply compiling the material at hand. As it is now, one has to read through a lengthy history and here and there he might find a casual reference to this [DOT]or that mineral, and in that shape the information is not available for practical men. I am pleased to learn that the minister contemplates so arranging things that he will be able to place in the hands of those interested, information as to the different minerals to be found in our country. It might be well that a special search should be made with a view of discovering certain minerals; for instance, a thorough exploration of the iron areas of our province. If a geological officer is merely sent to a certain district Hon. Mr. SIFTON.
to examine it in a general way it cannot be expected he will achieve such valuable results as would be obtained if a trained officer were sent there with the special object of devoting his whole time to one particular subject. That would be of the highest importance in Nova Scotia with reference to its iron and coal deposits.

That is quite in line with my own observation as the result of the work of the survey, and some of the best officers in the survey have practically said to me that while the general work of the survey should go on, yet at this present stage of development one of tbe most necessary things is to do that special work to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bell) refers. Dr. Barlow has been doing that in the case of nickel, and I think we should detail a competent officer to take up a certain mining field and to examine it thoroughly in its economic features and make a complete and full report about it, so that any person desiring to operate in that field would be in possession of all the information available. Such examination would be more detailed and complete than under a general survey. The coal fields of Nova Scotia are an illustration of tbe benefit of that kind of work. We have had Mr. Fletcher, who is well known to hon. gentlemen opposite, I suppose, and who has devoted practically his life to the study of coal in Nova Scotia. He would at once be detailed, with competent assistants, because he could not do all the work himself, to write a monograph on the subject of coal in Nova Scotia, and give us all the information he could get.
Who is in charge of the international boundary survey ?
Dr. Daly. He is a Canadian by birth originally educated in Canada and afterwards became a professor of Harvard University. He is a very capable man indeed.
I find in the Auditor General's Report that $1,065 was paid to D. R. Fletcher, of Vermont, for granite monuments to mark the boundary line.
We mark the boundary line with iron posts on granite foundations.

Perhaps it is that these were purchased by the United States authorities and that we are bound to share the cost, but if they were purchased by ourselves there is very good granite near where those posts were erected and we might have got it in our own country.
The cost was divided, but I do not know exactly how.
Who is the officer specially charged with the purchase of instruments V

The officer In charge of any instruments purchased in connection with the land survey, which has to do with the work of marking the boundaries, is not the same as the officer in charge of the purchase of instruments in connection with the geological survey. W. F. King, chief astronomer, has charge of all the boundary surveys, and any instruments required for that work would be purchased by him or on his recommendation. For the geological survey the acting director makes the purchases.
Then there are two separate officers to attend to the purchase of instruments. Is there any outside purchasing agent employed by the department ?
No, no such thing.

I mention the matter to the minister, because at the time the firm of Hearn & Harrison existed in Montreal, which has since gone into liquidaton, I heard something of a purchasing agent who resided in Montreal, and through whom all these instruments were alleged to he purchased, though he had no special knowledge of the subject.

I am glad my hon. friend has brought that matter to my attention, because there is absolutely nothing in the suggestion. There is nothing purchased for the Department of the Interior except on the requisition of the deputy minister, and his recommendation is made out by himself upon the recommendation of the officer in charge of the survey. As to recognizing any body outside the department as purchasing agent, or go-between, or anything of that kind, there is absolutely nothing of the kind, in any shape, form, or manner ; and the same thing is true of the geological survey, where all instruments are purchased on the recommendation of the acting director.
I am very glad to hear the hon. minister give us that assurance. What are the principal firms in Canada with which the department deals for the pur chase of these instruments ?
My deputy tells me that he thinks, speaking from recollection, that as a rule they have to be purchased in the United States. That is entirely so in regard to astronomical instruments.

Most of the purchases seem to be made in the United States, and I realize that for many instruments that may be necessary. But still I think that before dealing with American firms, it would be advisable to see if those who deal in similar instruments in Canada might not be able to furnish what the department re quired.

My hon. friend may rely on this, that we do not buy anything outside of Canada that we can get in Canada of equal quality, unless by oversight. Even in cases where the prices are a little higher in Canada, we still patronize Canadian dealers. Speaking from my own knowledge, I do not think there are any manufacturers of scientific instruments of the quality and class referred to in Canada with whom we could deal. Any dealers in Canada would be simply small dealers, with only a few instruments on hand. Of manufacturers I am satisfied there are none. '

The minister touched on a subject which I intended to make a little inquiry about. It is as to where one can get information most readily in regard to any particular mineral. The reason I ask the question is this. A gentleman came here with the view of finding where our iron deposits were and the nature of those deposits. I endeavoured to get the information for him, but found it almost impossible to get any. Is there any way in which that information could be got without much trouble ?
The MINISTER OF THE INTER iw . That is a matter which has been brought to my attention constantly for some years past. Our information, while in some respects very full, is in such a condition that it cannot be got at. In that respect my hon. friend is as well off as I am. If a gentleman came to my department and asked for information about iron, all I could do would be to call an officer to take him to the library of the geological survey, and show him the books in which he" could search ; and the probability is that he would not know muoh more after he got through than he did before. To remedy that defect would take some time ; but I am going to suggest a change with that object in view.

I sent this gentleman to the library ; but after searching through it, he said that life was too short to try to get the information from such an imperfect source, and he was afraid it was of little value to him. I thought there would be a complete list of the geological reports in the library, and some index kept up-to-date, so that one could ascertain at once where any of these minerals could be found, and in what volume they could be found. He said further, that even though he could get the information in these geological reports, it was very meagre. It might say whether the ore was magnetic iron or bog iron or sulphurous iron ; but it gave very little information beyond that as to the relative quantities of each, as to whether the deposits were large or small or as to the state of development. In all these respects this gentleman, who was from Pittsburg, said the geological survey was very im-

perfect; it was almost impossible to get any intelligent idea of it without a great deal of work. It seems to me that that could he remedied without very much trouble or expense, and I would suggest that the minister devise some way to overcome it, because it is a matter of importance, especially in view of the fact that our mineral deposits are attracting so much attention abroad, and that they are a valuable source of re-'*1'nue to the country.

I would like to make a suggestion to my hon. friend with reference to this item. ' I have received letters from different parts of the province of Quebec, requesting me to go to the geological department and try to obtain specimens of mineral, vegetable and animal life ; and I must say that in that department every effort is made to give us satisfaction. I think it would be of great use in the education of our people, if the minister could see his way clear to giving instructions to the exploring parties going out each year to secure as many specimens as possible, iu order that there should be gome for free distribution. In the province of Quebec we have ten or fifteen colleges maintaining natural history museums. It would be very easy, in most cases, for the officers, when proceeding with their explorations, to secure these specimens and reserve a certain quantity for the educational establishments who would make a demand for them. If that could be done without too much difficulty, the government could in that way enrich most of those educational establishments and diffuse knowledge throughout the country of its resources.

I do not see any serious difficulty in carrying out the suggestion of my hon. friend. To some extent it has already been done, but perhaps not as systematically as it might have been. I shall endeavour to carry out the suggestion.

From time to time we have had discussions regarding the propriety of building another museum, but have not heard much about it lately. Has anything been done lately in that connection V the museum building we have is quite inadequate.

I intend bringing this matter up when we are on the Public Works estimates, but in the meantime, as my hon. friend from Grey has introduced it, I should like to emphasize what he has said regarding the inadequacy of the present building. If hon. members would only visit the Geological Survey on Sussex street, they would be convinced that the building is a national disgrace, while at the same time they would be proud of the collections within its walls. Unfortunately, we cannot do justice to the many valuable specimens collected. Some most valuable Can-Mr. SPROTJLE.
adian mineral exhibits are stored away in boxes or on high shelves, obscured from sight, instead of being exposed to view. This state of affairs should not be allowed to continue. I would urge every member of parliament, who has not visited the Geological Survey, to do so, so that when we come to discuss the Public Works estimates, they will be able to give their views on this matter.

I have no dissent to offer to what my hon. friend has said. No one can doubt that we require a suitable building with the least possible delay. We intended proceeding last year, but there were differences of opinion regarding the site, and as this building will be a national museum, the question of site is an important one. The subject has been lately discussed by my colleagues, and I have no doubt that my hon. colleague, the Minister of Public Works, when his estimates are down, will make a full statement.

The hon. gentleman from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) has referred to a very important subject. There are some valuable collections in this country, and I think perhaps the Department of the Interior have been approached on the subject of purchasing them. It would be well for the department to secure these valuable collections, which are to be found throughout the country, and I trust the hon. gentleman will lose no time in doing so.
Has the government yet decided on the site ?

It has been definitely decided to construct the building and the delay has been due to the difficulty of deciding about the site. It has been suggested that the building should be erected in the park, and then other sites have been suggested. I am not in a position to make any statement, but no doubt the Minister of Public Works will do so. We hope to commence this year and will push the work forward with all rapidity.
I understand that some _ surveys were made with regard to locating coal in Prince Edward Island last year. Have the reports been furnished ?
Yes, I will bring down the report.
I notice that there was fi geologist sent down to the Sudbury district, where it is said there is coal. Has the government any definite information regarding that ?

The work of the geologist sent out to the neighbourhood of Sudbury had reference only to deposits of nickel. His report will be available shortly and will be printed

separately. I do not remember any report about coal in Sudbury.
I saw an item in the paper to the effect that the government had detailed a special officer to look into that question.
In the Sudbury district ?
Somewhere near Sudbury-in the nickel region.
I think the report is incorrect. There is no work of that kind done near Sudbury.
May I ask who it was who recommended the work of surveying for coal in Prince Edward Island ?
This was done on the recommendation first of the hon. member for East Queen's (Mr. MacKinnon).

A large expenditure was made by the local government a year or two ago just about the time of the elections there by this same gentleman. A large hole was bored, but without any result except that, possibly, the hon. gentleman gained some few votes by the distribution of the money. I cannot understand why, after a failure of this kind such a short time ago, the hon. Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) should undertake this needless expense in connection with his department, when he should have all the facts at his disposal. My knowledge of the geology of Prince Edward Island is not very extensive. I can only say that I received a communication from the hon. gentleman (Mr. MacKinnon) asking that this work be done. I referred the matter to Dr. Bell, and he recommended the work, and it was done accordingly. As to the details, I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lefurgey) will have to talk that matter over when the hon. member for East Queen's is here.
Mr.i LEFURGEY. I would like to have the hon. minister bring down the report at as early a day as possible.

I will bring it down at once.

There is an increase of $1,800 in this item. Will the hon. gentleman please explain ?
The MINISTER OF; THE INTERIOR. This vote is to enable us to catch up with work now in arrears. The maps were not got up as promptly as they ought to be. Since Dr. Bell took charge, to his credit be it said, he has endeavoured to get the work up to date, and this is a special vote to enable him to do so. He reports to me that this vote of $5,500, being an increase of $1,800 over that of 1902-3, is necessary because the vote of last year was insufficient to pay the salaries of draughtsmen employed for the fiscal year. Five draughtsmen are engaged, two at $3.25 a day, two at $3 a day, and one for eight months at. $2.75 a day, this officer being for the other four months engaged in field work and paid out of the general vote. Is the work tabulated in any way by these men, or do they simply do the work from the field-notes ?
They work from the field-notes of the technical officers.
The work the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sifton) spoke of a while ago would be further work in connection with analysing the results and putting them in tabular form.
This is different.
I understand. But that work of tabulating has never been done before ?

No. The only work of that kind that we have done has been the work that Dr. Barlow was doing last year. The work to be paid for by the vote now under discussion consists in putting in shape to be available the work of the technical officers in the field. The other work consists in collecting from the different reports of the survey

during the years it has been in existence the information which is embodied there, analysing it, casting out what is obsolete, perhaps making re-examinations to supplement the information where it is defective, and putting the whole thing in shape where it will be practically valuable to the ordinary reader.
If you are collecting this information, it can be done by these officers?
No. This is for technical office work necessary to make available the work done in the field.

But that gives no information. The hon. minister employs two classes of men, and he proposes to take a vote of $1,800 more than last year. That means that he will employ additional hands. What are those additional hands to work at ?

When an officer goes into the field and makes an examination of a certain district he makes his field-notes of the work he does. When he comes back he extends those field-notes, and then upon those field-notes are drawn the geological maps of the districts which he has surveyed. The preparation of the geological map is the work necessary in order to make available the work which the technical officer has done in the field. That is the foundation of the usefulness of the survey. That has been allowed to get behind, and we are trying to catch it up.

I want to call the attention of the minister to the case of Mr. Murray, who is an immigration agent stationed, I think, at Glasgow, or some part of Scotland. A complaint is made against him that he went out of his way to secure men to take the place of strikers at the Kingston Locomotive Works. Some correspondence took place, I believe, between the department and the Trades and Labour Hon. Mr. SIFTON.
Council of the Dominion, and the answers of the minister do not seem to be quite satisfactory, and I have been asked two or three times to bring the matter to his attention. On the 13th of October last, I received a letter from Mr. Kennedy, who is the corresponding secretary of the Toronto District Labour Council, which is as follows :-

Clarke, M.P., Toronto :
At the regular meeting of the Toronto District Labour Council, held September 11th, charges were presented to the effect that Mr. H. M. Murray, Canadian immigration officer at Glasgow, Scotland, had been co-operating with Mr. H. Tandy, of the Canadian Locomotive Works, Kingston, Ont., by advising machinists to go to Kingston, Ont., to secure work from the above firm, where the machinists were on strike. The matter was referred to the executive of the council to make a report. The executive met Monday evening, October 6th, and the sworn affidavit of Mr. H. Hunter, of Glasgow, was presented, together with copy of letter written by Mr. Murray to Mr. Tandy, introducing Mr. Hunter, which confirmed the charge as made to the council. The executive thereupon presented the inclosed resolution to the meeting of council held on the 9th instant which was unanimously adopted.
On behalf of the council, I ask your immediate support to make right the injustice done.
I remain.
Yours respectfully,
D. W. KENNEDY, Corresponding Secretary.
Follows a copy of the resolution passed by the Toronto District Labour Council, October 9th, 1902 :
That, whereas, it has been brought to the attention of this council that Mr. H. M. Murray, of the Dominion immigration service at Glasgow, Scotland, has been acting as agent for the Canadian Locomotive Works at Kingston, Ont., in securing machinists to take the places of the striking machinists at the above works ;
Therefore, be it resolved. That this body do enter its most emphatic protest against such conduct on the part of this or any other officer of the government as an unwarranted interference in a controversy with which he has, and should have, no connection, and as being most unfair, not only to those directly concerned but to organized labour in Canada generally.
And be it further resolved, That in the opinion of this Council the Hon. Clifford Sifton, the Minister of the Interior, should take immediate steps to have all correspondence between Mr. Murray, of Glasgow, Scotland, and Mr. Tandy, of the Canadian Locomotive Works, produced before the House of Commons, and if it can be proven that Mr. Murray was in any way aware of the existing trouble in Kingston, that we do most emphatically demand his removal from office.
And be it further resolved, That a copy of the foregoing be sent to the Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Hon. Clifford Sifton, Hon. William Muloclt, R. L. Borden, M.P., E. F. Clarke, M.P., E. B. Osier, M.P., A. E. Kemp, M.P., W. R. Brock] M.P., W. F. Maclean, M.P., and Archibald Campbell, M.P.

' He will be otherwise employed.' A general review of the conduct of the office led to the conclusion above referred to. I am not in a position to say ' that any one circumstance could be held to have been the deciding factor in the action taken.'
Yours faithfully,

Kennedy, Esq.,
59 Edward Street Toronto, Ont.
Mr. Kennedy has asked me to draw to the attention of the hon. gentleman these words which he claims are diplomatic, and he wants an explanation of their meaning :
' because it was thought that the duties could be more efficiently performed by another member of the staff;' 1 he will be otherwise employed;' 'that any one circumstance could be held to have been the deciding factor in the action taken.' These are the sentences that he has put within inverted commas.
I think my hon. friend would, himself find no difficulty in knowing what that meant.

The secretary of the Toronto Labour Council is very anxious for an explanation. There is a very serious question of principle involved In this matter. I do not think it should be the duty of immigration agents to interfere actively between employers and employees in Canada. I think if they do interfere they should state all the facts, such as are alluded to in the affidavit which accompanies this correspondence, and which was made by one of the men who came out to Canada through the instrumentality of Mr. Murray, and who was not made aware of the fact that labour troubles existed here or he never would have come. I had better read the report of the executive committee for the information of the hon. minister, so that the
matter can go on record, because I think we ought to have an expression from the hon. minister as to the policy which the hon. gentleman pursues and which he instructs his agents in the old country to pursue respecting this very matter. The executive committee of the Toronto District Labour Council made a report to the council. The complaint in regard to Mr. Murray's conduct was referred to the executive committee of the council and they took evidence, deliberated upon it and made a report as follows :
Office of the ' Toiler ',
October 17, 1902.
Executive Committee.
Your executive committee met in The Toiler office. Monday, September 29, to hear evidence substantiating the charge laid before the council by Mr. Boland, of the Machinists' Union, to the effect that Mr. Murray, immigration officer of the Dominion government at Glasgow, Scotland,
' had been acting as agent for the Canadian Locomotive Works of Kingston, Ontario, in securing machinists to take the places of the strikers at those works.'
The following members of the committee were present :	President Cox, Delegates Simpson,

Province of Ontario, County of York,
To wit :
