There is no difficulty about bringing correspondence down. I will have it prepared at once. My recollection of the circumstance to which the hon. gentleman refers is that when the complaint was made it was referred to Mr. Murray for his reply. My recollection of the conclusion at which I arrived, after examining the papers and hearing what Mr. Murray had to say, was that there was no positive proof that Mr. Murray did know all the circumstances of the case in Canada at the time when the event took place, but I also came to the conclusion that he had been, perhaps, a little careless in connection with the matter, and possibly that if he had been a little more alert he would have known. I think the circumstances are such that if he had been a little more alert and inquired into the circumstances this difficulty would not have arisen. The policy of the department and the instructions which the officers of the department have are that they are, under no circumstances, to promote the immigration of mechanics especially, and they are not, under any circumstances, to take part in promoting immigration from the old country of persons being imported for the purpose of taking the places of strikers.

What kind of reasoning has induced the minister to instruct his agents that mechanics are not to

be brought into this country. Is it because labour unions demand they shall not come.

Not necessarily, but because it has been the recognized view of the department that the expenditure of public money should not be incurred for the purpose of bringing mechanics to Canada. The justification of our expenditure lay in the fact that we were bringing people here who would engage in the development of our agricultural lands. I do not believe that any other policy could be sufficiently carried out. There are differences of opinion about the matter. My hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) has one opinion, fhe member for west Toronto (Mr. Clarke) has another, and the member for centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) expressed a very positive opinion the other day that we wanted 10,000 mechanics here, and that we wanted them right off.
Hear, hear.

I do not know that my hon. friend would say that if it should be the policy of the Immigration Department to bring them out, but he certainly expressed the opinion that we wanted mechanics here. I may say, however, to my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) that the labour unions do not dictate the policy of the government ; no one class of the community has the right to dictate the policy of the government, and yet I think it would be impracticable for any government to carry on a movement whereby mechanics would be brought in to compete in the labour market with the mechanics who are at present residing in Canada. I think that policy is impossible ; I do not think it can be carried out, and I certainly would not undertake to carry it out while I entertain the views I entertain at the present time. My hon. friend will understand that to err is human, and we have to work with human instruments, and perhaps sometimes a zealous immigration agent may not be as careful as he ought to be. But I can assure him that so far as the department is concerned the instruction which we give, and the views which we inculcate upon the officers of the department in that respect are distinct and definite and well understood. So far as Mr. Murray is concerned, I cannot say more than I said in the letter.
The complaint is that the letter is couched in very diplomatic language.

Well, it was intended to be couched in diplomatic language. The hon. gentleman will understand that when a minister is dealing with an officer who has been found not to be quite up to the job, it is difficult to express it in just the language which will accurately convey the idea. The history of
Mr. Murray's appointment is as follows : When I organized the work in Great Britain Mr. Murray was a steamship agent at Glasgow and had been in the service of steamship companies there for about twenty years. He was recommended to me as a very highly efficient and capable man of considerable experience and energy, and upon these recommendations, I paid him a high salary ; $2,000 a year. I was in Glasgow myself three years ago, and I saw Mr. Murray's work, and I conversed with other Canadians who had been there. His work was inspected by higher officers of the department and as a result, shortly after this occurrence took place, I came to the conclusion that he was not quite fit for the position there and I reduced his salary to $1,200 and put him in a less important place. If my hon. friend has employed men he probably has had occasion to do the same thing. The man who is now in office at Glasgow is Mr. Walker, a gentleman who was appointed to the service on the recommendation of the Minister of Customs. Mr. Walker is a newspaper man from Brantford, and possibly my hon. friend knows him. He is a very capable man, and I believe he will be a satisfactory officer.
What salary ?
And a house ?
No house.

There are some other matters in connection with immigration to which I wish to draw the attention of the minister. For the past three or four sessions I have quoted in this House statements made by United States officials respecting the quality of the immigration which is coming to Canada. I have drawn the attention of the minister again and again to the necessity for making a careful examination of our immigrants, because I think that quality must be taken into account as well as quantity ; and I may congratulate the minister that within the past six months steps have at last been taken to give effect to the suggestions that have from time to time been made from this side of the House, by the appointment of medical officers at the ports where these immigrants enter. But the statements are reiterated, at least in so far as they affect the fiscal year ending the 30th of June last, that the quality of the immigration coming into Canada is not such as we might congratulate ourselves upon. We should aim to emulate as far as we can the efforts of the United States government with regard to immigrants. We are congratulating ourselves upon the success which is attending the efforts of the minister and his officers, to increase the I number of immigrants that come into Cana-

da, and comparisons have been made of the numbers now coming, with those in previous years. But we must not forget that now-a-days the United States government is spending as much money to examine into the quality of immigration into the United States and to prevent undesirable immigrants from landing, as we are expending to bring immigrants to Canada, and that in view of the stringency of the regulations which exist on the other side it is a notorious fact
How are they endeavouring to restrict immigration ?
By the most rigid medical examination.
Is it any different now from what it was at the American seaports ?

Most decidedly. It is more stringent, and they have felt it necessary during the past few years to place this country in the humiliating position of having dozens of special immigration officers in Canadian cities, winnowing and sifting the immigrants that arrive in Canada destined for the United States, and declaring that such will be permitted to go into that country and that such will be refused entrance and may remain here without regard to what may become of them. I say that condition of things is disgraceful, and it is evidence to me that the quality of immigrants who come into Canada with the object of getting into the United States, is not such as we should desire to retain here.
What is the difference in the inspection at the American seaports now from what it was before ?

I am trying to tell the hon. gentleman and the committee that the examination has become so rigorous, that it is alleged by American officials that thousands of immigrants from Europe who could not pass the United States inspection, come by way of Canada, the United States being their destination, in the hope that having resided in Canada for some little time, and being made familiar with the ropes, if I may use that expression, they can find their way across the border into the United States. The American government, becoming apprised of that fact, were obliged, in order that the same rigid inspection might take place along the Canadian border, to appoint dozens of officers. They have now I do not know how many dozens of officers extending along the border, all the way from the eastern seaboard to Seattle, and they are appointing more this year, so that the same rigid examination may be given to immigrants going to the United States via Canada. They do not hesitate to refuse permission to enter the United States to immigrants who cannot Mr. CLARKE.
pass their standard of examination ; and these immigrants, at all events, until recently, have been left on our hands, and have been in some cases a source of considerable expense either to municipalities or to the country generally.
Has the hon. gentleman any definite information ?
I will give the hon. gentleman definite information if he will keep his seat for a few minutes.
And the places where they may be found ?

There is not a place in Canada where the United States government have officials, where they cannot be found by the dozen. If the hon. gentleman will look into the matter himself, he will find abundant evidence of what I am saying. I think it is my duty to draw the attention of the hon. minister to these statements, so that he may investigate them, and take means to remedy the evil complained of, and to have the same rigid examination at our seaports as takes place at the seaports of the United States. The document I am about to quote from is Senate document No. 62 :
Report of the Committee on Immigration, United States Senate, on the Bill (H.R. 12199) to regulate the Immigration of Aliens into the United States, with Statements before the Committee in the First and Second Sessions of the Fifty-seventh Congress.
This document, I presume, can be obtained in the library. At any rate, it is open to the inspection of the minister or of any other hon. gentleman on either side of the House who desires to peruse it. I was so struck with many of the statements made in it that I thought I would be derelict in my duty if I did not draw the attention of the hon. minister and of the country to the condition of things which is alleged to exist, or to have continued to exist until the 30tli of June last. Mr. Watchorn was examined before the committee, and at page 439 of this document, I find this statement made by him in reply to a question of the chairman :
Now, turn if you please, to page 7 in the report of the immigrant inspector in charge of Canadian border inspection for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1902, and you will see that out of 4,900 immigrants which we have examined in ten months at various points along the Canadian border, from Sault Ste. Marie, Mich., eastward to St. Johns, N.B., 2,028 were found to be of the inadmissible classes, and of that number 496 were suffering from loathsome or contagious diseases, 812 were paupers, and there were 10 insane, 8 idiots, and 5 ex-convicts.
Hon. gentlemen may try to explain away these statements, and I would be very glad if satisfactory explanations could be given of them.
What became of them ?

Let the hon. gentleman inquire of the immigration officers here. I cannot tell what became of them. . Those in humble circumstances, I presume, did not return. I think it is a serious matter, and a matter worthy of being inquired into. Further on, at the same page, the same gentleman makes this statement:
When you come to realize, gentlemen, that with the very best force of inspectors the government can employ at these stations, yet out of the 600,000 immigrants coming into all the ports of the United States those 600,000 furnished a less number of cases of loathsome or contagious diseases than the 5,000 who came in, or attempted to come in, over the Canadian border, you will see that the work on the Canadian border is simply an auxiliary to the work at the American ports ; and if you are going to exempt the transportation lines which carry them in from the penalties which attach to the steamship companies bringing them to the ports of the United States, it is a complete nullification of the work.
I think hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House will admit that this is a very serious statement, and that it ought to be investigated ; or, if it has been, the hon. minister or his officers ought to give some explanation with regard to it.
What is the date of that report ?

December 20, 1902 :
In the Senate of the United States, December 20, 1902.
Ordered, that Senate Report No. 2119. Fifty-seventh Congress, first session, together with the hearings before the Committee on Immigration, in the first and second sessions of the Fifty-seventh Congress, be printed as a document, and that so many extra copies he printed as will not exceed in cost the sum of $500.
Attest :	CHARLES G. BENNETT,
Secretary.
That is the attest on the inside page of the cover. Further on, at page 441, in reply to a question from Senator McLaurin, of Mississippi :
Senator McLAURIN, of Mississippi. Then, Mr. Watchorn, is it a fact that the vessel landing at a port of Canada is compelled to pay the same amount of head tax that a vessel landing immigrants at one of the ports of the United States pays ?
If the people they carry go to the States, they do.
If they are coming to the United States ?

Yes, sir.
That is to say, these Canadian or British ships that are bringing immigrants to Canada for the United States have to pay the head or poll tax which the United States government imposes on ships bringing immigrants to United States ports. They collect from the vessels coming in a sufficient sum to maintain the immigration department. Further on, speaking about these steamship lines, Mr. Watchorn says :
I ought to say that the lines coming to New York, Philadelphia and Boston have medical examinations in Europe.
They do not like to have to carry back a great many people and swell their record of deportations, and as a matter of self-interest they examine medically at all European ports and weed them out. They say, 'You cannot go,' and ' You cannot go,' and so they stand them off, twenty and thirty, sometimes a hundred on a ship, and the very moment they stand them aside, the lines that run into Canada gather them up and put them on a ship to Quebec. So it comes to pass, as you will find if you turn to the Commissioner General's report, on page nine, column five, that there is a very small percentage of loathsome or contagious diseases rejected at American ports. You will see what a very small percentage they represent of the whole number carried. Now, turn to page 11 and look at the list of the border ports until you get down to Montreal, and you will find that of 737 total rejections at the Montreal office no less than 388 were suffering from loathsome or contagious diseases. In other words, not one-tenth of one per cent of those hi ought to American ports are diseased, while as many as sixty per cent of those brought to Canada are suffering from these diseases.
I would suggest to my bon. friend from Western Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) tbat be should pursue an investigation as to wbat became of these 737 immigrants^ who were rejected at Montreal by the United States medical officer. It would be a fruitful subject of inquiry, because at that time there was no provision made, as I understand, for their examination by an officer of the Canadian government. These officers, I understand, were appointed in December last.
During what year were these rejected, and what were the causes of rejection ?

You will find in the Commissioner General's Report page 9-I presume for 1902-that not one-tenth of one per cent of the immigrants brought to American ports were diseased, while as many as sixty per cent of those brought to Canada were suffering from trachoma and other loathsome diseases. Surely we have no reason to rejoice in the increased number of immigrants coming to our shores, if the unfortunates are diseased before getting on shipboard on the other side.
The Commissioner General being fully aware of these facts

That is of the quality of immigrants coming into Canada

Sent me over to Chiasso, Italy, where all this sifting out work is done, to see how they managed it. I found that when an immigrant comes to Chiasso. and to the Switzerland border, he is there examined medically, just as thoroughly as at any port of the world. If he is found to be diseased the agents says to him * it is utterly useless to sell you a ticket to New York, and T must sell you a ticket to Quebec. You cannot get into the United States any other way hut you must bide your time in Canada and take your chances and get over the border. He singles these people out and puts

a certain label on the lapels of their coats. If it is a red and white label it signifies to the agents at the European ports, when they arrive there that in no sense must you sell this man a ticket to the States, but put him on ship going to Quebec.
At page 443 he goes on to speak about the smuggling of these immigrants from Canada to the United States. There have been plans and schemes devised at Montreal to run these immigrants into the United States clandestinely or to smuggle them in :
In all cases where an immigrant is brought over by a smuggler you do not accord that immigrant the right to go back to Canada and receive medical treatment, as they do when they originally apply, but take him at once through a warrant issued by the Commissioner General, to New York and send him back at the government's expense to Europe. We are sending back batches of them every week in this manner.
Let me now read something which, 1 think, is not a matter we may congratulate the hon. minister upon. It has reference to the law which was passed respecting the inspection of immigrants :
The chairman said1 : I wish you would touch on the efficiency of the new Canadian regulations as to immigration.
They have passed a law in Canada by virtue of our work on the border because we /have, as it were, stemmed the stream and it is now flowing back to them. They, for the first time in their history, have taken cognizance of it and have passed a law to prevent people of this kind, from coming into Canada ; but have not yet adopted sufficient machinery to put it in operation, and hence they keep coming. As it stands now. Senator, I get hold of a dozen or twenty of these men who are diseased. I write a letter to the commissioner of immigration for Canada and I call attention to their act and tell him there are twenty people now in the vicinity of my office suffering from loathsome or contagious diseases. Then he sends au officer, who comes and takes them away and nuts them on a ship and sends them out.
The Chairman. Would the Canadian law be effective if there was machinery to execute ?
Mr. Watchorn. Yes ; it would, because it would keep this class of people out.
The Chairman. Are its provisions modelled on the same features as ours as to those ineligible to be admitted ?
Mr. Watchorn-Only so far as pertains to disease. They will not keep out paupers. They want immigrants too badly for that. Here is the certificate as it is issued by our force at the port of arrival in Canada.
Senator McLaurin, of Mississippi. Is that the same certificate printed in your report ?
'Mr. Watchorn. Yes, sir. There is a place, you will observe, provided at the bottom for the signature of the inspector who takes up the card and the date on which he takes it up, I think it attests amply the efficiency of the border force when I tell you that out of 26,000 certificates of that kind issued last year we picked up 25,980 of them.
So careful and exact is the examination of these American officials, so thoroughly and systematically do they do their work, that out of these 26,000 permits, which they Mr. CLARKE.
gave people coming through Canada to enter the United States, they were able to collect _ at the border no less than 25,980.
My hon. friend from Lennox has handed me a letter, which I will read in this connection, to show the necessity for even more stringent regulations. I do not think that the fact that a man is poor should deprive him of the right to come into Canada and make a home for himself and family, but people who are diseased should not be allowed to enter and be a burden on our taxpayers. We should not be put to the expense of maintaining them in charitable institutions weeks and months until they have quite recovered. That class of immigration ought to be discouraged, but no effective steps have been taken to bar it out. The hon. Minister of the Interior should impose a poll tax on each immigrant that our steamship agents bring to Canada and keep that money for the purpose of meeting the necessary expense of treating diseased immigrants. If there should be no diseased immigrants, the money could be refunded. To show that the class of immigration that is still coming in is not as desirable as it should be, let me read a letter addressed to my hon. friend from Lennox:
Montreal, July 15, 1903. Uriah Wilson, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons, Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-Allow me to extend to you my thanks for drawing the attention of the people to the matter of immigration.
I have been trying for the past year to arouse some interest in our city, which by the way is the chief sufferer in regard to this evil. If it would do any good I would be only too glad to travel to Ottawa to have an interview with some of the members who are interested in this subject.
I have the honour to remain,
Yours truly,

It is hardly fair that the philanthropic and benevolent people of great centres, such as Montreal, should have the care and maintenance of diseased foreigners imposed on them as well as the care of their own indigent and sick. I think that this letter is quite sufficient to justify me in making a strong statement as to the desirability of putting a stop to the immigration into Canada of people suffering from disease.
There is one more extract which I propose to submit to the committee for the information of the hon. gentleman. It is taken from the statement of M'\ A. S. Anderson, passenger manager, American Line International Navigation Company, Philadelphia :
In order to show that the old influences are still at work in Europe to Induce aliens to evade the United States immigration laws by taking the route via Canada, I will read you a letter from our passenger manager in Antwerp, dated May 24th, 1902 :
' I Inclose a memo, of our agents, Blank & Co. It shows that the rate of the Beaver Line

is francs 125 to Quebec, francs 137 to Montreal, and to New York probably higher. Our rate to New York is francs 125. I further inclose a statement of passengers that passed here. Considering that our rate is cheaper, our boats faster, superior, and sail direct, the question comes up. Why are they so successful 7 The question is answered by the memorandum, in which Blank & Co. say : ' We give to the Beaver Line only the deficient passengers.' That is the secret of the Beaver Line's .large carryings. All the passengers who have -been rejected at an Italian port, or who are deficient, or who have reasons to take advantage of the 1 Landing without inspection,' and prefer the certainty to the risk, travel by the Beaver Line.'
The immigrants referred to as passing Antwerp for the Beaver Line during April and May number 1,113.
I commend this to the attention of the hon. minister and the committee. I do not vouch for the statements contained in it, but this is an official document, a report of the evidence taken before the United States Senate Committee. I think I was in duty bound to bring this to the attention of the hon. minister and of this committee, because it is absolutely essential, now that the United States are discouraging immigration, and uow that the tide of immigration is coming our way-and I hope that the tide of eligible immigrants will increase in volume every year-that every reasonable precaution should be taken to see to it that the diseased and criminal classes shall be kept out of this country; and any reasonable sum required should be voted, and I am sure will be voted, by this parliament, to attain that object. Personally, I am pleased to see that the hon. gentleman has already appointed special officers at Montreal and St. John-I think he included St. John-and Halifax. I hope that he will give instructions to these officers to redouble their vigilance, and that every reasonable step will be taken to prevent ineligible persons getting on board the steamships at the ports across the Atlantic. Prevention will be found to be better than cure; better prevent these people getting on the ocean steamship rather than have them deported or interned in Canadian hospitals for three or four weeks after they reach here. And, if the hon. minister adopts a more rigorous course than has been followed for several years past, when we meet again in this House we shall not find statements of this kind from the immigration officers of the United States, and will be able to congratulate ourselves that, while the stream of immigration is increasing, the quality is improving. I regret having been compiled to take up the time of the committee in reading these documents, but as I ga.ve notice the other day that I would bring this information before the committee, I must ask hon. members to accept that notice as my apology.

I cannot add much to what I have already
stated to the committee during the two or three days when this subject has been before us off and on. I can only say that, after looking into the matter last year, I appointed a medical inspector for the department to rigorously supervise the landing of all immigrants. The instructions given are of the strictest character. If any objection is made that the officer is not carefully and efficiently carrying out his instruction, l should be happy to make a thorough investigation; and, in view of what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) has said, without anything further, I intend to make a thorough investigation as to whether or not he is carrying out the instructions. I believe he is. I do not speak from personal knowledge, but I intend, in view of what has been said, to be able to speak from personal knowledge or as nearly that as may be possible under the circumstances. I may say that 89,000 immigrants have arrived at ocean ports since the medical inspector began his work in December, some 700 of whom had been either rejected or detained for treatment. That is as nearly as possible the proportion in the case of United States immigrants. The total number deported or detained at the various ports of the United States during the last year was 4,974, which bears about the same relation to their total number, 048,000, as 700 would to our total of 89,000. I find also, if I may be allowed to cite the witness whom hon. gentlemen opposite have cited against me, that the United States inspector at Montreal, who has lately been interviewed, says that our inspection is even stricter 1hrn that of the United States. So my hon. friend. (Mr. Clarke) will at least have some satisfaction in knowing that we are moving in the direction he suggests. I find that the United States inspector, whose name has been quoted in this debate a number of times, says that, while he has at times criticised the action of the Department of the Interior, he is bound to acknowledge that we have rejected proportionately more than the United States on account of the diseases mentioned.
More come this way.

But he says that we reject proportionately more on account of trachoma. The hon. gentleman can hardly maintain that more are coming this way if his argument is, as I understand it. that diseased people seek to come through Canada to the United States.
No.
That was his argument.

I pointed out that on the other side of the ocean, at Antwerp and these other ports of embarkation, intending immigrants who are not able to pass a satisfactory medical examination were not allow-

ed to embark on steamships bound for the United States ports, but were ticketed for Canada.

But if they were ticketed for Canada and subsequently intended to go into the United States-for that is the whole burden of the report quoted by the hon. gentleman-there would necessarily be a large proportion of diseased persons trying to get in from Canada over the American border. I shall not argue the point ; but the hon. gentleman will know that the United States inspector himself in whom my hon. friends opposite appear to have great confidence, says that the inspectors of my department at the present time are rejecting more than the United States inspectors. I simply cite that as evidence of the fact that we are trying to make the inspection as thorough and careful as possible. We recognize the necessity of this, and I very cheerfully give my undertaking to the committee that everything possible will be done to have this work of inspection satisfactorily carried on.

Before leaving this matter. I would call the attention of the hon. minister to the charts which accompany the report of the Commissioner General of Immigration of the United States. I think if the hon. gentleman would prepare charts to accompany his annual report similar to those which are found in the appendix of the United States report, they would convey very valuable information to the people of Canada, and enable them to judge as to the quality of the immigration coming into the country.
My hon. friend is referring to those charts in the report of the Commissioner General ?
Yes.

I want to say a few words which I intended to say the other night. I mentioned that the immigrants coming in were not of as desirable a class as we would like, and I understood that my statement was contradicted by the Minister of the Interior. My hon. friend from Montreal made reference to it as well, and I believe the statement he made was contradicted. I want to say that for the last few years our country is becoming literally overrun by a class of men who are little better than tramps, Russian Jew pedlars, Poles and Italians, with little packs that they carry about with them, are going all over our country. Many of them degenerate into tramps in a very short time ; and in our section of the country, at least, you cannot go in any direction without you meet these men, either getting off a train, or walking along the roads, going into houses, leaving the gates open, begging for meals. They have a little pack with them as an excuse for going from place to place. These men

are allowed to come in as immigrants. They are undesirable immigrants, because they do not belong to the industrial classes of the country. They make their living purely by deception in peddling, selling something which may be stolen in some other part of the country, and selling it for an exorbitant price to the innocent people who buy it. That is one class. Now, with regard to diseased immigrants who come in. The minister says that his department is entitled to credit for what it has done. It is true they appointed an inspector at the frontier last December, and if the country is receiving any benefit from that to-day, it is the opposition who are entitled to the credit and not the government. It is said that the inspectors stop these diseased people from coming in, and the minister said that the few who did come in were stopped at the border and treated until they were cured. He says that this is not an incurable disease and only requires a short time to be cured. I said nothing about this subject the other night, because there were others who desired to take up the time. I desire to say to the minister that every medical man knows that these cases of trachoma are practically incurable particularly when it reaches a chronic stage. Every medical man knows how hard it is, if not impossible, to cure it.
Would the hon. gentleman give us some idea of the nature of the disease ?

The disease is called granular inflammation of the eyelids, and when it continues for a long time it is almost impossible to cure. The minister told us the other night that he was assured by his officers that it was curable. Out of curiosity, I went out into the library and brought in an authority. I have here 'Swan-zy, Handbook of Diseases of the Eye.' He is a standard authority on this subject. Speaking of the disease of trachoma, he says of its prognosis :
At any period prior to cicatrisation of the conjunctiva an attack of purulent blennorrhosa is liable to come on. If not too severe this may result in a cure by absorption of the trachoma bodies, and should not be checked. If, however, the attack be very severe the eye runs dangers similar to those of an ordinary attack of purulent conjunctivitis. These dangers are less the more complete and the more intense the pannus.
On the whole, if the disease come under treatment at an early period, it may be hoped that vision will be retained in. a majority of cases, although a radical cure may be difficult or impossible.
Now, it is a fact, as every medical man knows, that when these cases become chronic, it Is difficult and almost impossible to cure them. Thousands of them are never cured.
These cases require to be under constant or intermitting treatment for long periods, often ' for years, and are extremely liable to relapses.

Wliat is the date of that work ?
Mi-. SPROULE. If it would be of any use to the hon. member to know, it was written in 1897. He will see that it is very recent, and if he has any curiosity to see it, I will send it over to him. It is later, I presume, than the date when the hon. gentleman got his education in this particular line. I want to say that I have seen many cases of immigrants coming in, and havfe treated some of them, and I know how difficult it is to treat this disease successfully. Immigrants so affected are dangerous to those who are associated with them, either in the wash room or in the sleeping room, or otherwise. Up to last December practically there was no effort made to stop these people coming into the country, but owing to the incessant criticism of the opposition, the government have at last appointed an inspector at Montreal to keep them out. Now the hon. gentleman cheers himself over the statement of the American officer who said that the Canadian officer was rejecting more than the Americans were. But he forgot to tell us that the Americans rejected them at two points; first they rejected them when making the selection, a place where the Canadians do not reject them. Therefore, there is a larger percentage of diseased persons coming into Canada than of those going to the United States, and the rejections are consequently more numerous here than there. 1 say this medical man was sent none too soon to Montreal. Another word with regard to immigration. I was in Winnipeg a short time ago, and I saw that the preparations made by the government for receiving and handling immigrants are entirely inadequate. There is not enough room provided for their accommodation.
Which port ?

At Winnipeg. I am not complaining so much of that, because the number coming is so large that It might be quite impossible to expect much from that, but I am only drawing attention to it so that some remedy may be found, and I think it ought to be found at the earliest possible date.

I understand that the hon. minister is reducing the number of agents at work in the United States. Will he give an explanation of the work they have been doing ? I mean those to whom commissions are paid.	[DOT]

Some years ago, when we were starting the work in the United States, endeavouring to get it under way, and to get as much interest taken in it as possible, it was considered advisable to appoint a large number of sub-agents on commission. These men received no salary, but they were paid a commission on the number of people they sent. The persons directly despatched by their efforts signed certificates, which were collected later on by the officers in the Northwest, and forwarded to the department here, and the commissions were paid on these certificates. As the work progressed and the number of salaried agents increased, and they became more fully acquainted with the work, it was considered advisable to cut off the appointment of these sub-agents on commission. Some time last year the inspector reported that it would be advisable to discontinue their appointment, and all the sub-agents were removed and their appointments cancelled. Since that time, some forty or fifty of them, who were considered to be of some value, were re-appointed. The other day I gave a list of the subagents who had earned any commissions, with the amounts they had earned. That is about the way the matter stands at present.

Will the minister explain how it comes that when he had a large number of agents in the United States who were receiving commissions on settlers coming into Canada was less than it is now, when he has fewer agents ?

I have already explained that our officers went to the United States and picked out men willing to accept these appointments, for the purpose of infusing interest in the work and getting it under way. Later on, when the work was developed, finding that a large number of the sub-agents had not done anything to justify their appointment, their appointments were cancelled. The time spent in this work, however, was not lost. In the first year that we appointed agents, only 700 or 800 people came. Since that time the number has increased. The appointment of these sub-agents, so far as we can learn, did not result in any particular benefit to the country, and that is the reason why we discontinued them except in a few cases. They did not cost the country anything, however, because they did not earn any commissions.
Some did earn commissions. I notice that one, William Ritchie, received $4,559.
He was only paid on the number he got.

I understand that the commission was $3 per head for men over eighteen years of age, $2 per head for women, and $1 per head for children under eighteen. The minister having cancelled the appointments of all the sub-agents, does he purpose continuing that policy next year ? Looking over the report, it would seem as if these local agents in the United States simply came to a central point and got into communication with the railway company, and received their commission on the people coming from the United States to Canada without having done any work at all. Does the hon. gentleman purpose continuing next year those he reappointed ? If I understood him correctly, some few were reappointed on the same work last year.

I can only say that it depends on the cir-sumstances of each case. The territory in which we are doing our work is very large. If the inspector thinks any particular man should continue in his appointment, he is kept on. It is altogether likely some will be kept on because they happen to be men who are doing^good work. At the end of another year, our inspecting officers may report that it is not desirable to continue them in office any longer.

I notice in the Auditor General's Report that one or two are appointed for each state in the union. I would understand by that that a man would not be permitted to do any work outside of his own territory. In the Auditor General's Report, one man last year was paid $1,979- N. Bartholomew. In what part of the United States did he work ?
Somewhere between the St. Paul office and the Omaha office.
Did he not work in Iowa ?
I think for a part of the time.
I understood the hon. gentleman to say that a lot of those men were dismissed from office. There is a large number here. $48,701 were paid in bonuses.
I gave the name of every agent the other day in the discussion, and how much he earned.

Referring to some very interesting data given by the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Clarke) regarding medical inspection, I quoted a day or two ago a newspaper report to the effect that Dr. Faber, inspector at Quebec, is an American practitioner, whose right to practice in Quebec has been called in question by the College of Physicians and Surgeons of that province. He seems to have been appointed by a steamship company to look after immigrants suffering from trachoma and detained in the city of Quebec. How did these immigrants get through quarantine ? That question is one of considerable interest because we have in the city of Montreal people suffering from trachoma, and one would like to know how these immigrants got there. Are the officers appointed to inspect the immigrants all qualified practitioners and what are their salaries ? And where are they placed in order to perform that inspection. I might add that many immigrants remain in Montreal and are a very sickly lot indeed, even without this affection of the eyes. Many of them are by no means satisfactory as regards their moral conduct. Those who succeed in gaining a living in tire city of Montreal are, most of them, simply parasites. Those who work stand in the way of our workmen getting a fair wage, because they work for almost nothing. They do not live at all as our labourers do,



they work for very low wages. That is the reason, probably, why this immigration is so very unpopular among the working classes of Montreal. It would be impossible to find a single labour organization in the city of Montreal that would approve of the kind of immigrants that have been passed through that city within the past five or six years. I should be glad if the minister Would give us some information with regard to this class of immigrants.

The procedure, when the immigrant lands at the ocean port is this :	The ship is
boarded first by the quarantine officer, who is an officer of the Department of Agriculture, not of the Department of the Interior. The quarantine work is carried on under the direction of Dr. Montizambert, director general of public health. When the Inquiry with regard to the disease of trachoma was brought up, we were advised by the Department of Health that trachoma was not a quarantinable disease. So, the ship is not quarantined because of any of the passengers being affected with trachoma. Nor are passengers necessarily prevented from landing because they have that disease. The passengers are all inspected before they land, by our medical inspector, and in any case where the medical inspector thinks the disease is curable, the party is detained for treatment. Before they are allowed to depart from the House of detention at the ocean port they must be cured to the satisfaction of our inspector. The medical inspector of the department, Dr. Ellis, of St. John, gets a salary of $2,000 a year. He was appointed last year, and the general instructions Issued to him are to examine immigrants arriving at the port, all Canadian bound immigrants and also all immigrants proceeding direct to the United States, but not passed by the American inspector. He is to order the deportation of all American bound immigrants afflicted with loathsome or contagious disease. If the immigrant is suffering from some simple, non-contagious disease, or if he has only some slight physical defect not sufficient to prevent him from earning a livelihood in the ordinary way he is not excluded. In case of parties suffering from curable disease who have sufficient to pay their expenses, he may permit them to enter a hospital, where they are to be kept until they are cured and there is no danger from infection. In case of immigrants who are unfit to proceed upon their journey and who refuse to enter the hospital, he is to order their deportation. So, hon. gentlemen will see that, so far as the instructions are concerned they cover the case fully, and I think it will be found that since the present machinery has been provided under the direction of Dr. Ellis the inspection has been pretty thorough. My hon. friend will remember an interview that I read this after-Mr. MONK.	'i
noon in which the American inspector at Montreal said that the medical inspectors of our department were more strict than his own.

My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Sifton) will excuse me if I insist a little on this point. My excuse is that I do not believe in the system of assisted immigration at all. I have to bow to the policy which my hon. friend has adopted, but I believe in selected immigration, and I think this assisted immigration is not only a great mistake, but is going to give us a great deal of trouble before very long. Therefore, my hon. friend must be indulgent with me if I ask a few questions. A great many of these Immigrants reach Montreal on board ship, which comes up from the gulf to the port of Montreal. They disembark there and take the train for the west. Has the department an inspector at Montreal, and, if so, who is that inspector ?
The inspection has been carried on under the direction of Dr. Ellis without the appointment of a permanent officer until lately. Dr. Stewart is the permanent officer now.
Does the inspector attend upon the arrival of every batch of immigrants to perform his duty of inspector ?

Those are his instructions. Our inspector is not Dr. Stewart, the eminent physician, with whose name my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) must be very familiar. At least I do not think it is. The appointment was recommended by one of my colleagues in Montreal. I know the inspector simply as Dr. Stewart.
Has the inspector a regular salary ?
I think he is paid by fees.

It would be very desirable to have an inspector in Montreal who would attend upon the arrival of every ship containing immigrants. My hon. friend will bear in mind, speaking of the disease which has been mentioned so often
The number of immigrants who land at the port *<of Montreal are comparatively few.
We see a great many of them there.
The principal landing places are Halifax. St. John and Quebec. The number landing in Montreal, is, comparatively speaking, very few.
We see a great many disembark from the ship at Montreal.

I mean the steerage passenger's to Montreal

are very few. It would be hardly worth while to have a salaried officer there.
I find the name of a Mr. W. J. White in the Auditor General's Report. Is he an immigration agent ?
He is general inspector of immigration agents in the United States. He inspects the work of the agents and supervises the work of advertising and the preparation and circulation of literature.
It seems to me that living must be very high In the United States. I see this gentleman is allowed for sixty-one days, at $10 per day for living expenses. What part of the United States is he in ?

Mr. White has had large experience in connection with the subjects of advertising and dealing with the press, and he was taken to England by the deputy minister for the purpose of overhauling the immigration work in England. He was given an allowance of $10 a day for his expenses while he was there.
The inspector of immigration agencies had to be taken to Great Britain. What did you want him there for 7

Mr. White was taken to England by the deputy minister because a considerable portion of the work which the deputy minister undertook to do there was to secure proper attention to that work by the British press, and in the matter of approaching the press and securing proper press recognition, Mr. White is a specialist. In the Department of Immigration we had no other officer so competent, and I am bound to say he was very successful.

Does it cost any more for a specialist to live in England than to live in Canada 7 That is almost enough to support the minister himself, $10 a day. Then we have $384 for fares. Does the department supply all their officials with valises and traps of that sort 7 If they do, I would like to get a job. I do not think the people of this country should be called upon to pay these men extravagant salaries, to pay them $10 a day for their living allowances, and $384 for fares. I suppose they travelled in pullmans and staterooms. It may be very nice for ministers that have political friends to attend to, but I think the electors of this country will take it more seriously. We have sums all through the Auditor General's Report. There is another gentleman here, I would like to know if he is an agent, too, in the Immigration Department, a gentleman by the name of W. W. Cory. What is that gentleman's business 7 * 215}

Mr1. SCOTT. Mr. Chairman, I respectfully ask for your ruling on the point of order I raised. The hon. gentleman is discussing an official who is not an immigration official, and has nothing to do with that department.

gration. It would not be In order, and would not be according to the arrangement, to discuss any question outside of immigration. Therefore I call attention to the fact that we expect every one to confine his remarks to some phase of the immigration question.
I had your ruling before that I was in order, and the Minister of the Interior said he might as well give the information now as any other time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

I thought it was well understood, and I think the Minister of the Interior understood, that any item might be taken up on the question of immigration. The other items were permitted to go through with that understanding. speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I must disagree with what you have just stated, Mr. Chairman, that we can only discuss immigration items. I think the item we are now discussing includes a great deal more than immigration, and we are perfectly justified in discussing any question which comes under item number thirty.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When I said the committee were only permitted to discuss questions of immigration, I meant all the questions that come under the department of the Minister of Interior. But they cannot discuss any question that is outside of his department, no matter what the Minister of the Interior says, because he has no power to give privileges to the committee outside of his own department. As long as the discussion is confined to dealing with the various questions of the Department of the Interior, it will be allowed.

I have to inform you, Mr. Chairman, that you are out of order, because this gentleman is in the Department of the Interior. We are talking about Mr. W. W. Cory, page L-41 of the Audi-to General's Report. This Mr. Cory, I understand, is inspector of land agencies in the North-west and In the Yukon. For that service he is paid $2,400 a year, a very liberal allowance. Then this gentleman for bring expenses in the North-west Territories and In the Yukon gets $620. He gets for fares $384. I suppose he is travelling in luxurious coaches and pullman cars, and all that sort of thing. Not only that, but he pays $31 Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER,
for a valise that sost $25 and some other traps that he has to carry around cost $8.50. Then he gets a $3.50 leather purse. An ordinary purse will not hold his money. I suppose it so bulges out that he must have a leather one to hold it. He gets $20 for tips. What is that for ? I have had several definitions of that on this side of the House, but I have not received a ministerial explanation. Are the electors to pay their money out for gentlemen that are travelling around the country, for valises and three or four bags of different kinds, for a $3.50 leather purse and for tips to the amount of $20 ? This gentleman's trip cost us $4,204.10. I think that is a pretty serious matter.
You might have called it even money.
What is my hon. friend saying ?
I was merely saying that my hon. friend might have called it even money and knocked off that ten cents.

I wanted to be particular, just like the hon. gentleman was when he protested against the Indians being inspected by a doctor. Here is the amount of money that is paid to one man, and I think this is something that should receive our consideration. Why should it cost $10 a day to live in the North-west Territories ? I know the hon. minister feels away down in his heart that there must be a fraud in connection with that. No man, if he is living as he should and if he is honest in his report, would pay $10 a day for living in the North-west Territories. I think it is shameful that the country should pay that amount of money to any man. It does not cost a man of ability any more than it costs ordinary mortals, and if there are men who want to live as high as that, I think it is better that they should be discharged, because I am satisfied this is a fraud that is perpetrated on the public. Why should we pay for this gentleman's valises and purses? I should think he could pay for his own, and I do not think the hon. minister will justify this. His second epistle might, but I do not think be would.

The truth about Mr. Corey is that be gets his actual expenses while in the North-west TeiTitories. In the Yukon he gets $200 a month for his living allowance. The living allowance of the ordinary officer in the Yukon is $150 a month. This gentleman is an inspector travelling all the time, and from the best information we can get we believe that $200 a month is no more than a fair living allowance for him While in the Yukon. It would be quite Impossible for the government to get along without an inspector. We have a large number of officers handling large sums of money, and the only check -the government has is the report of the in-
<3857

specter, who goes from office to office and makes a detailed report in regard to the affairs of the offices he visits. We must have a competent man for that duty.
Do you fit out all your officials for such trips as tills ? Do you buy their clothing, too ?
No ; we do not buy their clothing.
Do you furnish all your officials with valises and bags ?
The department is required to furnish a despatch bag for the official papers that they require to carry.

I would like to say a few words In regard to immigration from the western states and from Europe. I do not pretend to find any fault with what the hon. minister has done or what he is doing, but, at the same time, I may say that the hon. minister does not go at that kind of business as I would do it myself. I do not think he is going at it in the right way. In the first place, we all know that it is a poor class of people who leave Ontario and Quebec and the other provinces, men who have not sufficient means to go to the west and who get no help from the government at ali. The Canadian Pacific Railway gives them some help, but I never knew a case in which the government helped any of these people. If they have done so, I have never heard of it. We all know the poor class of people are the men who desire to go to the west. The rich class of people do not go there, and if you ask a wealthy man to migrate to the west the reply you will get would be : I am not compelled to ; I can stay at home. If you put the same question to a man without means, the reply you would get would be this : Well, give me the means and I will go. He is perfectly right in saying that. A man with $25. $50 or $100 is not able to go there and make a home for himself, unless he wants to make a slave of himself. A man should have means sufficient to enable him to live a year at least, and these people, having no means, cannot go to the west ; and, as a matter of fact, they do not go. A great deal has been said about Canadians emigrating to the United States. It is very easy to condemn them in the House here, and to say that they should not go to the United States, that they should do this or that, but you must remember it is not so easy to carry out the advice that is given to them in this House. Very few hon. members of this House know what emigration means. A man with a few dollars, three or four dollors, or perhaps ' ten or fifteen dollars, when he gets hard up, can go to the United States. We must remember that a poor man in Quebec can go to the United States at a cost of a few dollars, whereas it costs him
a good deal more than he can afford to move to western Canada. In the States our people get work and save a few hundred dollars, and then they return home and others go to take their places, so that it is a case of going and coming all the time. The money spent on immigration is not spent in the right direction. It is a disgrace to see how our Canadians are being allowed to drift to the States. You see train load and train load of them moving off, and the next day an agent starts off after them to try and coax them back again. If you took the money that was spent on their going and returning, and the money that you spend on the agents, and the money that you pay for bringing here the trash of Europe, and apply the aggregate amount to keeping our own Canadians at home you would be spending money to better advantage. I know something about the west, because I was there before half of you were born, and forty-five years ago I walked right up to the Pembina Mountain. I could have bought half of the west at that time for little money, but the trouble is that I hadn't the money and like other poor folk I had to come back. It is just as well for the minister to stop his agencies in the United States or else to change his system. Previous to 1862 there were very few Canadians in the United States and there were comparatively few factories, but during the civil war the men were engaged at the front and as the women took their places in different employments the Americans came over here and succeeded in inducing a number of our younger people to settle down there. They got $45 and $50 a month, but as it required $2.5(j in paper money to get one dollar in gold the people were not anxious to leave the States and so they stayed there. That was really the beginning of the Canadian settlement in the United States. If the Minister of the Interior gave more encouragement to Canadians to stay at home and less encouragement to Europeans to come here he would save money and have a better class of population in Canada.

I have listened attentively to this discussion on immigration which lias been going on for four days, and I think I may say that no one will accuse me of taking up the time of the House by engaging unduly in the discussion. In reply to my hon. friend (Mr. Morin) I would say that while doubtless it is true that so long as the world lasts there may always be improvements suggested in any system which is being carried on by human agency, still when we look at the results of the work which is being carried on by the Minister of the Interior in connection with immigration, we must admit that it is producing good results; at all events vastly better results than were obtained when the Conservatives were in power and were conducting

their policy of immigration. 15very member of this committee will admit that it is most important that we should receive in Canada a good class of immigrants. We do not want diseased persons nor those who might be classed as paupers and who are liable to become a burden on the taxpayers. The hon. gentleman from Toronto (Air. Clarke) discussed the question this afternoon with commendable moderation, and his words bore that great weight which his words always bear when he speaks in this House. Yet I think that perhaps he laid too much stress on the report of the United States officials which would go to show that over 700 diseased immigrants had necessarily been left in Canada within a certain period. I was constrained to ask him where these people had gone to, and the hon. gentleman advised me to institute an inquiry to discover. I think, Sir, that most hon. gentlemen will agree with me that the suggestion of the hon. gentleman was in itself an answer to the complaint he was making. If it be necessary to institute an exhaustive inquiry to discover where these 700 diseased persons have found a haven of rest in Canada, we may take it for granted that the condition of things is not so serious as he would make out.

I would ask the hon. gentleman to look up the record of ' Hansard,' and he will see that quite elaborate explanations were given as to where these people have been going and what a burden they were on the municipalities. Surely he would not expect me to ascertain where the seven hundred who were rejected went ? I merely drew attention to the statement that this number were rejected at a single Canadian port by-the officials of the United States. There was no means of our sending them back ; that is the position.

I have listened to practically all the discussion that has taken place on this subject in the last four days, and until the hon. gentleman himself presented a letter from a gentleman in Montreal this afternoon, we had not one item of definite, practical information on which to base a complaint Even the letter which the hon. gentleman read was very vague. The gentleman wrote as follows :
Allow me to extend to you my. thanks for drawing the attention of the people to the matter of immigration. I have been trying for the rast year to arouse some interest in our city, which by the way is the chief sufferer in regard to this evil.
Evidently the matter is not considered very serious in the city of Montreal, if he has been trying for a year to arouse some interest in it, apparently without much success. He goes on to say that he would be glad to come to Ottawa if his presence would be of any benefit. That is the first practical item of evidence which has been Mr. SCOTT.
given to the House that there was any real complaint. I venture to say again that if there is difficulty in discovering the location of the complaint, and if an exhaustive and close inquiry is required this would go a considerable length in proving that the complaint is not very serious. As a resident of the North-west Territories, where a very large proportion of the immigrants go to, I may say that I am as much interested as any member of this committee in that question as to whether diseased persons or undesirable characters shall be permitted to come into this country. Speaking as a resident of the North-west who has within recent years come into contact with a good many of the new settlers, I may say that in our country there is no serious complaint at all against the character of the immigrants. There is not to my knowledge any considerable number of them with loathsome diseases or with any class of disease. AAritb regard to the people who have come from Europe, I have never heard a single complaint on that score. The only complaint with regard to incoming settlers has been with regard to some of the people who came from the United States, who, a few days after their arrival, developed cases of small-pox. The disease was not developed when they came aeross the border and were examined by the physicians there. While I am on my feet, I would like to say that it must be a matter of very great satisfaction to the House and the country generally that, in the matter of immigration, we have got to the point where we can feel that we can afford to discriminate and sift. Until a few years ago it was never suggested that we ought to sift ; the whole cry was to get people, any kind of people, to come to the country. Only the year before the election of 1896, when the hon. gentleman's friends were in power, this problem of immigration was considered so serious by the people of this country that a great convention was called, held in the city of Winnipeg, I think, in February, 1895 or 1896, at which there were delegates from all points between the Pacific coast and lake Superior.
Promoted largely by Conservatives.

Promoted, as my hon. friend says, largely by Conservatives. It was attended by the then Minister of the Interior, the Hon. Mr. Daly, who begged the delegates to suggest some means to him by which he could induce people to come to this country. The feeling of that convention was almost one of hopelessness about bringing immigrants into the country to help to develop its resources. Until my hon. friend the present Minister of the Interior took office and took charge of the Immigration Department, we never had any reasonable amount of success in dealing with this pro-

blem. I agree entirely with my hon. friend from centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) who spoke on this subject a couple of nights ago, that the general policy of the government has far more to do with a solution of this question of immigration than anything that may be directly done by the Immigration Department. My hon. friend knows that I entirely disagree with him as to what that general policy should be, particularly on the question of the tariff ; and if my hon. friend looks back over the history of recent years, he cannot fail to reach the conclusion that the policy of the present government witli regard to the tariff and transportation-
Is the hon. gentleman in order now ?

I am perfectly willing to submit to the ruling of the Chairman. This is a phase of the question which was discussed at considerable length on another day, this week. I do not wish to take up any length of time in discussing it. I merely wish to say that I agree wholly with the hon. member for centre Toronto in the belief that the general policy is the more important consideration.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman will tell how far the Minister of the Interior altered the tariff policy in actual practice with regard to the North-west Territories ?

I am afraid my hon. friend is trying to lead me into a wider discussion of the tariff. That has been pretty well thrashed out in this session and in recent sessions. I would only refer my hon. friend to his leader, who stated with reference to the iron duties that enormous reductions had been made since the present government came into office. I repeat that I entirely agree with the hon. member for Centre Toronto in that regard, and I was going on to say that if he would look over the history of' the recent past, he could not fail to arrive at the conclusion that the present general policy of the government, as well as the very ' effective immigration policy which has been put into operation by the present Minister of the Interior, is proving to be a notable success, at least as compared with what we had in previous years. In the year 1890, the total immigration had been reduced to about 16,000 a year, as a result of the general policy and the lack of an immigration policy on the part of the hon. gentleman's friends who were in office.
How much was spent during that year in promoting immigration ?
I believe ?120,000.
How much was spent last year ?
Between $500,000 and $600,000. But I would point out to my hon. friend that in previous years the Conservative government spent a vastly larger sum than $120,000.
You are referring to 1896. Stick to your text.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Hon. members addressing the committee should stand and address the Chair.
I must apologize, Mr. Chairman, for having transgressed the rules.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This whole discussion is irregular. We have discussed this question three consecutive days.
