You have no right to dictate to us.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am not dictating, but simply showing why the whole discussion is irregular. Should any hon. member call my attention to the rule and say that we are not bound by any arrangement made between hon. members on both sides, I will be forced to declare this discussion out of order.
We have no objection to your declaring what the rules of the House are; but when you undertake to dictate to us how we are to discuss these matters, you are entirely out of your sphere.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must always dictate to hon. members when a point of order is raised. I am pointing out in what respect this discussion is out of order, and when the hon. gentleman discusses the ruling of the Chair, he is committing a breach of order himself.
We have legal redress in this House.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has no right to discuss the ruling of the Chair.
I am resorting to the redress I have in common with every other hon. member.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman wishes to appeal from the ruling of the Chair, he is at liberty to do so.
I will do that if you will persist in dictating to us what we shall do.

As the original offender, I most humbly apologize for having transgressed any rule. I was endeavouring to proceed strictly with the discussion of this immigration item which is now before the committee. I was dealing with the contention advanced by my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Clarke) that the expenditure
6S63

of the late government was only $120,000 per year. That was the expenditure In 1890, but during the ten years from 1881 to 1891, there was a considerably larger annual expenditure; and the reports of the Immigration Department showed a very satisfactory return in the way of immigration, the figures being in the vicinity of 800,000 people. But when the census enumerators however-those very zealous enumerators to whom the lion. Minister of Trade and Commerce sometimes refers-took the census in 1891, it was discovered that not only had we not retained the S00,000 people we had brought in at an enormous expense, but had scarcely maintained the natural increase of the country. But the conditions are now entirely altered. We have been getting during recent years a very considerable number of immigrants; and although it has been insinuated time and again during this debate that we are not keeping them, the figures and facts show the contrary. Every person is aware that we are retaining the people brought into the country and the fact does not require to be fortified with the proofs in order to be convinced of it. Last year the production of Manitoba and the North-west Territories increased to an enormous total, exceeding 126,000,000 bushels of grain.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Thanks to a kind Providence.
Was Providence never kind during the whole eighteen years when the hon. gentleman's friends were in power.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Yes.
How much of that prosperity-was due to the presence of such immigrants as the Doukhobors ?
A very considerable proportion.
How much ?
The settlements of the Doukhobors shows a very considerable production.
Give us the figures.

I have not got the figures at hand, but I can tell my hon. friend that, from what I know, the Doukhobor and the Galician settlements are proving very successful, many of these people are just as successful and valuable as new settlers as any of the others brought into the country, but I would remind my boil, friend that it was not the present government which began to bring Galicians into the country. Before 1896 the great efforts of the Immigration Department were devoted to countries like Galicia.
The hon. gentleman has introduced the subject of Galician immigration, which I did not mention at all. We must not build up houses of cards to knock them down again.
Does the hon. gentleman object to my introducing the subject ?

I object to iny hon. friend dragging me into it. I did not mention the subject of Galician immigration. If he wants to make an argument in favour of Galician immigration, let him do so, but not in reply to me.
Then I take it that, as far as the hon. gentleman is concerned, he withdraws all the objections urged in past years to the Galician immigration.

Surely the hon. gentleman must submit to the intelligence and common sense of his auditors. I asked him to explain what proportion of the prosperity of Manitoba and the North-west Territories is due to the presence of the Doukhobors. If he wants to ascertain what opinions are held of the Galicians, I must refer him to the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver). I did not even mention them.

I have not got the figures of the actual production of the Doukhobor settlements, but if my hon. friend will take my word, speaking as a resident of the North-west Territories, my best information is that the majority of the Doukhobors are proving very good producers and settlers.
I am very glad to hear it.

There was a considerable number last year who were seized by some mania and gave considerable trouble, but that trouble lias been almost entirely removed. There is a very limited number who are still affected by this form of mania, and a couple of dozen of them are incarcerated in some of our institutions at present. I would remind my hon, friend also that the Doukhobors came into the country under different conditions from any of the other classes. They did not come in through any efforts of the Immigration Department but at the request and under the auspices of the Society of Friends of the United States and Great Britain.
Why then did the Immigration Department take credit for bringing these people out ?

Does the hon. gentleman think that the Immigration Department would have been justified in excluding the figures of the Doukhobors from its returns ? Is the department not in duty bound to include in its returns all the people who may come in during any one year. However, Mr. Chairman, I was proceeding to point out to the hon. gentleman that the difference in results is shown by the conditions in Manitoba and the North-west, and I was quoting the enormous total production of grain last year which exceeded 126,000,000 bushels. I have not under my hand figures showing the total production in the year 1896 or previous years, but I venture to

state that the production last year was fully three times as great as it was in any year prior to 1897. Then, take the figures with regard to the export of cattle.
Was that increased export due to the immigration policy of the government ?
Very considerably. The increased production of grain and cattle-
Cattle ?

Yes, it was certainly due to the increased population of the country. My hou. friend (Mr. Clarke) surely will not contend that the same number of people as in 1896 increased the production to what it was last year, fully four times as great as that of 1896 or any prior year. In 1896 the total export of cattle amounted to
8.000	head. Last year we exported to Great Britain alone, 41,000 head, besides very considerable exports to the British Columbia mining markets and to the Yukon. Then I would direct his attention to the transactions in land in that country, which are a very good index of the general business conditions. In the year 1896, the sales of the Canadian Pacific lands amounted to a total of 66,000 acres, representing about $200,000; and the total sales of all the companies exceeded by very little 100,000 acres for a sum in the neighbourhood of $245,000. In a single month during the present year, the Canadian Pacific Railway sells more land than all the companies together sold in any year prior to 1897. Last month the Canadian Pacific Railway sold between 300,000 and
400.000	acres of land, these transactions re-presentingmorethan $1,000,000, and the total sales of that company last year amounted to about 2,500,000 acres for a total of almost $10,000,000. The conditions go to prove the contention of my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) that the general policy pursued by the government has more to do with immigration than anything that can be done, directly as an immigration policy. The immigration policy that we pursue bears about the same relation to the whole conduct of government as the advertising and bookkeeping departments of an ordinary business bears to the whole business. It is a necessary and valuable element, and the business could hardly be conducted without it. I am inclined to agree with the Minister of the Interior that it is necessary to make these expenditures directly upon immigration, and to advertise our country throughout the world, so that we may induce people to come here and assist us in developing the country. But the Immigration business itself is only a small factoi-, the main factor being such a policy on the part of the government as shall make the conditions of life in the country so favourable that people will be induced to come, and to stay when they have come. As I pointed out to my hon. friend, in years gone by, we got large
numbers of people, but they refused to stay. The conditions of life in the western country under the policy pursued up to 1S96 were such that these people could not make a living, and they refused to stay.
What is the difference In the conditions ?
The ordinary farmer
In what way have the conditions improved ?

If my hon. friend will be patient, I will tell him. The conditions with regard to tariff taxation were so severe and the freight rates imposed by the Canadian Pacific Railway which hon. gentlemen opposite had constructed
Will the hon. gentleman so far insult the intelligence of this committee as to say that taxation is now less than it was in 1896 ?
Certainly it is. The rate of taxation is very considerably lighter than it was in 1896. And if my hon. friend disputes it, I will refer him to his own leader who will tell him what I tell him.

Our leader never contended anything of the kind. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) makes no distinction between taxation and duty. We admit that some duties are reduced, but taxation has increased and the burdens of the people of the west are increased.
I am willing that my hou. friend (Mr. Henderson) or any other gentleman should go to the western farmer and endeavour to convince him
Will the hon. gentleman permit me to interrupt him again ? Will he tell us what lines of goods are cheaper than in 1896. Coal oil?-binder twine ?
This is not in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regard this, at least, as outside the question.

I am obliged to tell my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) that lam not a travelling price list. But he has always shown himself a fair-minded man on the floor of this House, and I think he is fair enough and his range of knowledge is wide enough to enable him to agree with me when I say that the whole conditions of livelihood in Manitoba and the North-west at all events- those countries I know something about- are vastly more favourable to comfort and success than they were in 1896.

I am always willing to take any of the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Scott's) statements that appeal to my judgment: and I should be glad to take his statement now, but that I have seen, and compared, and compiled figures that compel me to express a doubt as to the accuracy

of what lie is saying. That is the reason I asked him for the figures. I assert that taxation is higher now than it was in 1896. I ask him how the conditions of life are improved, so far as the government could improve them ? Will he say that the cost of living is lower ?

My hon. friend and I will have to agree to disagree. My opinion is that taxation is not higher than it was. The farmer buys numbers of articles which he is compelled to buy, at less rates to-day than prior to 1896. Practically all lines of clothing come in at lower rates than prior to 1896, and every important feature of the business of gaining a livelihood in that country has been made more favourable to the farmer. One very important feature is the reduction of freight rates.
By the Manitoba government.

By the present Dominion government. One very material reduction, as the hon. gentleman knows, was that brought about by the Crow's Nest Pass contract, made, if I remember well, in the year 1898. Then, the whole administration of the department over which my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior presides is more intelligent, more energetic and more satisfactory to the people, since he has taken hold of it, than was the case before. My hon. friend from Toronto has been in the North-west and these things must be within his knowledge. In countless ways which would take too long for me to enumerate- my hon. friend from East Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane) would become impatient were I to go over the list-the conditions of life have been vastly improved, as the result of the policy of the present government. And the results are shown by the figures which prove that the people are coming into that country, and not only coming in but staying there. As I said before, according to reports of the Immigration Department, we received under the administration of hon. gentlemen opposite 800,000 people in ten years. But they did not remain in that country. I venture to say, on my responsibility as a member of this House that, in the year 1896, there were not to be found in Manitoba and the North-west one out of every five, of the people who had originally gone into that country. Why had they gone away ? They were driven out by the non-intelligent policy adopted and carried out by the Conservative government up to 1S96. The conditions to-day are entirely different. Does anybody dispute that they were driven out-that they went out ?
Nobody doubts that they were driven out, but they were driven out by the cries of hon. gentlemen oppposit? that this country was not fit to live in..

I would advise my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) to tell that to the mar-Mr. CLARKE.
ines. That is well enough to say here, but it would be absolutely useless for him to attempt to convince the people of Manitoba and the North-west of anything of that kind. In the early years of 1890 a considerable immigration set into the Northwest from the western states of the union, directed chiefly to northern Alberta. These people found the conditions of that country such that they remained less than four years ; and if hon. gentlemen will look over the files of western newspapers for the years 1891 and 1895, they will find accounts of the caravans of these western settlers who were travelling south again, going back to the United States, too poor to pay railway fares. The conditions were such that they could not sell their effects, their wagons and their horses, and the only way to get out of the country was to hitch their teams to canvas wagons and drive hundreds of miles to reach their old homes. I will give hon. gentlemen one instance. In 1895 it was expected, in the early part of the year, that a general election was about to take place, and the parties commenced to prepare in the various districts. In a little settlement east of Regina, the settlement of Balgonie, very largely composed of people from Europe, a class similar in some respects, particularly in their industry and thrift to the Galicians, called Germans, or Russian-Germans, descendants of people who nearly a century ago migrated from Germany to Russia, in that settlement the voters' list was made up in the year 1895, and the election was held in June, 1896. Now let hon. gentlemen bear this fact in mind, that when that election was held in June, 1896, it was found that there were ninety less voters than had been put upon the voters' list in 1895 ; ninety voters representing ninety families, had pulled up stakes and gone away to the United States, because they could not make a satisfactory living. To-day the majority of these people are back on their old holdings in the Balgonie district.
Would the hon. gentleman repeat again the statement he made with respect to the expenditure on immigration under the old government and under the new government ?

I said that in 1896 the old government spent $120,000, and that in former years they had spent sums vastly greater than that, and they were also bringing in immigrants in greater numbers, but those immigrants did not stay in the country.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that the Liberal-Conservative government expended a sum vastly greater than the sums expended by the present government since 1896 ?

No, I said that in certain years the Conservative government spent sums almost as great as the sum exjmnd-

ed by my hon. friend the present Minister of the Interior last year.

I would like that question to be put right, and I would refer the hon. gentleman to the Year-book, and ask him to read the figures, also give us the years when the Liberal-Conservative government spent anything like $65,000. Perhaps the bon. gentleman would be good enough to read us the figures for the five years prior to the defeat of the Liberal-Conservative government, in 1806, backward, and then take the years forward from 1896 up to the present year.

I prefer to take the years for the period of which I was speaking, which was the period from 1881 to 1891. The expenditure in 1881 was $214,251 ; in 1882, $215,339 ; in 18S4, $511,209. I had not looked at these figures for months, and I was speaking from recollection when I said that in certain years the Conservative government had spent almost as much money as my hon. friend did last year.
Read forward from that year.

In 1885 the hon. gentleman's friends spent $423,861. I think these figures substantiate the statement I made that there were certain years when his friends spent almost as much money as was spent by the present government last year. Now, before concluding my remarks, I would like to give my hon. friends opposite some advice. I think they are prepared to admit that on the whole the immigration problem has been fairly and satisfactorily solved by this government, and if they are not prepared to admit it, I may say that at all events the people in the west are satisfied with the administration of the Immigration department by my hon. friend the present Minister of the interior. What was the position last year ? Up to the 30th of June last, we had an immigration of a little over 126,uUO. Something in the neighbourhood of 45,000 of these came from the United States, and hon. gentlemen on both sides admit that these are first-class settlers. Then we got from Great Britain about 41,000. The balance of these people came from the various countries in Europe, and the Minister of the Interior, or his officials, inform us that about 6,000 of these people came from Galicia, were of that class of people known as the abused Galicians. Let us admit for a moment that the Galicians are objectionable. And we have to admit that, with the exception of this 6,000, the whole of these 126,000 new settlers that came into the country are of the very best class we could desire. I think that is fair proof that immigration is being dealt with to the general satisfaction, even of the most captious critics who sit upon the opposition benches. Now, I must allude to a slanderous remark that was made by the hon. member for
East Grey (Mr. Sproule), who, I am sorry to see, is not in his seat, against the Barr colonists. I think my hon. friends opposite will generally admit, that I am stating the case fairly in saying that they do not object to immigrants from the United States nor from Great Britain, except possibly some individual cases. But the hon. member for East Grey made a slanderous and abusive remark against the Barr colonists, against those 2,500 people who came out here. He said he learned that there were rumours afloat that these people were composed of the scum of the London slums. Now I say upon my responsibility as a member that sucb a remark is a slander; and I can quote from the statement which was already quoted by my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) in this House, made by Mr. Haul-tain, in the legislative assembly at Regina, that the Barr colonists were as a whole as fine a class of people as ever came across the water. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) read to this House an extract form the speech made by Mr. Haultain, who said he had travelled with a number of these people and had never seen a finer class of settlers. I say it is a shame and a disgrace, and an abuse of the privileges of this House, for an hon. member to get up and make such a statement without a semblance of authority. When put to the proof and asked what he had to justify his remarks, the hon. gentleman said that he thought he had seen it in some newspaper. He was not even able to state the name of the newspaper. I think I am in the judgment of the House when I say that no hon. member has the right to make such a remark about any class of people in this country, whether they are new comers or old timers, without the best justification, and all the justification the hon. member for East Grey had for calling the Barr colonists scum from the London slums was the statement that he thought he had seen it in some newspaper. I venture to say it was a newspaper without any semblance of authority if the hon. gentleman really did see it in any newspaper. I will read from the hon. gentleman's speech on the floor of this House.
What day was that 1 I do not remember when the hon. member for East Grey spoke.
It was just a week ago tonight.

this evening carrying out, against the rules of the House, an arrangement that was made between the committee and the minister. I am not going to permit every rule of the House to be violated because these arrangements have been entered into.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I move that the committee rise and report progress and ask leave to sit again. I do this because it is evident that lion, gentlemen opposite have been obstructing the passing of these estimates for the last hour or so. Hon. gentlemen on this side of the House have a number of questions to ask and it is impossible for us to ask them until the government supporters stop obstructing.

It is now in order for me to make a few remarks. I may say to the hon. member. (Mr. Scott) that I do not wish to take his place, but, I have to take a train in a few moments. I call liis attention to the quality of immigrants coming into this country. I will not quote from a previous debate, hut I would direct his attention to a speech made by the Minister of Agriculture the other night as to the exodus, and I am sure the member for Assiniboia will not challenge the statement of the Minister of Agriculture.
Not at all. I am aware of the figures he gave.
Do you concur in the statement of the minister ?
The statement was made with reference to the eastern provinces.
Very well then, these figures reveal a condition of things that ought for ever to shut hon. gentlemen's mouths as to the exodus.
The exodus in the west has entirely ceased.

Let me tell the hon. gentleman that twelve months ago the Minister of Agriculture made a speech in which he proved to our satisfaction and to his own that between 1890 and 1895, 43,000 Canadians went to Massachusetts, and between 1895 and 1900 there were 41,000
Will my hon. friend permit me

Wait till I have finished the sentence-the later period during which the hon. member (Mr. Scott) would like to persuade us that the exodus had practically ceased-now then the Minister of Agriculture may say what he has to say.

The hon. gentleman is not correctly quoting what I said the other night. I was correcting a statement made by the leader of the opposition and the question was as to the number of Canadian born people in the state of Massachusetts. That statement does not show that they went from Canada to .Massachusetts ; they may have come from any other part of the United States to Massachusetts. The hon. member for Pictou last year made a statement to this House in which he quoted incorrect statements from the American returns. I corrected that misstatement. The other night the leader of the opposition quoted the incorrect figures of the hon. member for Pictou given last year, and I showed that I had refuted that misstatement of the member for Pictou. What I said was that these people were Canadian born living in Massachusetts at these dates. They may have gone there from Canada or anywhere else.

Let me point out to the minister that the figures quoted as to the number of Canadians in Massachusetts between 1890 and 1895 were made'to do duty to show the enormous exodus from Canada during that five years period ; and when we apply the same rule to the Minister of Agriculture he says : Oh, but these Canadians may have been residing in some other state of the union and may have gone from that other state to Massachusetts. If the hon. gentleman thinks that the explanation meets the situation, I have no objection to the Minister of Agriculture having it placed on record. This afternoon the member for Assiniboia made the statement that 700 was the total number of diseased immigrants rejected in Canada by the United States officials. I quoted the statement of Mr. Watchorn that in one year in one port 737 immigrants who came to Canada ostensibly to go to the United States had been rejected ; but if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) will turn to page 11 of the annual report of the Commissioner General of Immigration for the fiscal year ending June 30th, 1902. he will find a tabulated statement, No. 3 ; ' report of immigrants refused admission from foreign contiguous territory to the United States under provision of the Alien Contract Labour Laws and Laws Regulating Emigration ; ' and he will find that all told there were 2,016 and not 737 rejected at the United States border. So long as that condition of things is per-Mr. CLARKE.
mitted to exist; so long as that percentage of unsuitable immigrants is allowed to come into this country, the hon. gentleman cannot make any boast as to what has been done by the Interior department.
In introducing this matter this afternoon, it was for the sole object of drawing the attention of the hon. minister to the statements again and again made by the immigration officers of the United States as to the quality of these immigrants, and of urging the minister to take steps to prevent the introduction of this class of people into our country. The hon. gentleman refers to the number of immigrants coming from the United States into Canada. Why have they come, though it costs more to live here now than it did five or six years ago ? Because the available land of the United States is practically taken up, and because they can buy in our North-west for $3 or $4 an acre just as good land as they left in the United States, and can sell the land they left for five or six times that price. The hon. gentleman knows, of course, that the immigration from the United States is very largely induced by American land speculators who have bought large blocks of land in the territories and are advertising in whole-page advertisements in' the newspapers of the United States the superlative advantages of our North-west as a country for settlement. And if the immigration from the United States was not as great formerly as it is to-day; that was due to two facts : First, there was available land for settlement in the United States ; and next, the hon. gentleman's friends never ceased to decry the North-west country, publishing the most pessimistic statements respecting it; and because, further, the conditions of life had not been solved by the settlers to the same extent as now. The experimental stage was not past then. It is happily past now, and the series of abundant harvests which the country has enjoyed in the past few years has done more to attract attention to its advantages, and to induce immigration to flow into it than all the efforts that have been put forth by the Minister of the Interior and his friends in the government.
Motion of Mr. Taylor negatived :	yeas,
21; nays, 25.

In reply to the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), who I am very sorry is compelled to go away, I may say that I entirely agree with him that this inspection and keeping out of diseased persons is most important. I trust that there is no member of this committee who desires to see diseased or undesirable persons allowed to come into this country. But my point was that I thought the hon. gentlemen opposite were laying undue stress upon this matter. At all events, speaking for the people of Manitoba and the North-west Territories, I said that there was practically no complaint in that country, to which the

majority of our immigration goes, on this score. But before this little interruption occurred, which 1 very much regret, 1 was dealing with the abuse which at present and for years past has been showered by hon. gentlemen opposite on all classes of people who have been coming into Manitoba and the North-west Territories-abuse which in all cases has been unjustified. For years the Minister of the Interior was assailed because a large number of people were coming from Europe and a comparatively small number from Great Britain. But we find, from the remark which I quoted from the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproulc), that they are quite as ready to abuse people coming from Great Britain as they were those coming from Galicia. If the hon. gentleman was disposed to be fair, he could have quoted the testimony of the Prime Minister of the territories, a member in good standing of the Conservative party, as to the splendid character of these Barr colonists. He could also have quoted the testimony of a Conservative newspaper published in Battleford, which I may say is the pioneer paper of the North-west Territories, and whose editor was no doubt very familiar with what he was writing because all these colonists went through Battleford on their way to the locality where they settled. That paper spoke in the very highest terms of the character of those people. I wish again to offer to my hon. friends opposite a word of advice regarding the statements which they sometimes purposely make and sometimes, 1 am fain to think they carelessly make, in abuse of the new settlers. For instance, the other evening, in speaking in this debate, the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) spoke of the government permitting to come and settle on our fertile lands of the Northwest Territories, idiots, insane persons, diseased persons, and paupers. His remarks might easily be construed into a reflection on the majority of the people who have come and settled in the country.
Do not misconstrue them. I did not say that they settled on the lands of the North-west Territories. I said they were rejected and remained in the country.

I am endeavouring to point out to hon. gentlemen opposite the advisability of their being a little more careful in the statements they make with regard to the people who come into this country. I do not think the hon. gentleman intended any reflection on a majority of the people who come and settle in the country, but he did speak about idiots, insane persons, diseased persons and paupers being permitted to come to this country, and that remark might well be construed into a reflection on the people from the United States and the people from Great Britain who have come in during the past year. I am certain that
the hon. gentleman intended no such reflection, and I merely point out that it would be well for hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House to have a care of the way they speak about those people. I quite agree with what the hon. Minister of the Interior said the other night, that man for man a better lot of people never came into the country than the 125,000 who came in during the past year. Forty thousand came from the United States, nearly an equal number from Great Britain, and the remainder from other countries in Europe.
I would like to make a reference to the Galicians, chiefly because of a reference made to them by one of the other members from the North-west Territories the other night. I may say that I do not at all agree with the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) in his estimate of the Galicians as settlers.
Would the hon. gentleman have the hardihood to say that if the hon. member for Alberta were in his seat ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: He took good care to look around to see that he was not there.

It will be the privilege of the hon. gentleman for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) to draw the attention of the hon. member for Alberta to my remarks in ' Hansard.' I have frequently said the same thing to himself, and I am sorry he is not in his seat to listen to the remarks I have to make. It would not be news to him. He is perfectly well aware of my opinion. In my opinion these 6,000 Galicians who came into this country during the preceding twelve months are valuable and useful settlers and are welcome among us, and an equal number next year and the following years will receive from the great majority of the people of Manitoba and the North-west Territories an equal welcome. The hon. member for Alberta does not express the unanimous opinion of the people of his own community. The Conservative newspaper in the town of Edmonton has frequently given testimony to the good character of the Galicians, and I might quote also the testimony of the Conservative mem-mer for the district of Victoria in the Northwest Legislature in their favour. And as that gentleman is a merchant in the town of Fort Saskatchewan he has ample opportunities of judging. The hon. member for East Grey took considerable credit this afternoon for the efforts of the opposition in keeping a certain number of undesirable characters out of the country during recent months. Had he gone back to the years before 1896, he would have found that his party friends were successful in keeping hundreds of thousands of'people away from this country. If we had had in those years the intelligent progressive policy we now enjoy, we would not at present have but

a paltry quarter of a million in our western territories, but something near a million and a half. Speaking as a representative of the territories, I can assure the hon. Minister of the Interior that his land admistration, his immigration administration, and his administration of the various other branches of the department, meet with the very warm endorsatlon of our western country.

I do not wish to enter into a discussion of the record of the two political parties, on which my hon. friend has detained the House the last hour and a half, but I wish to draw attention to one point at issue between the hon. member and myself. He tried to create the impression that the Liberal-Conservative party had expended nearly as much money upon Immigration as the present government. I wish to correct that statement.
I said that in certain years the hon. gentleman's friends had spent almost as much as we did last year.

I do not know what the hon. gentleman means by that, except that he would like to leave the impression that at certain times the late Liberal-Conservative government had expended as much money on immigration as this government. I will take any six years the hon. gentleman chooses during the eighteen years when the Liberal-Conservative party were in office and compare them with the six j'ears of the present administration, and the comparison will show which of us is right. But if the hon. gentleman will not name any six years, let me take the last six years of the late administration, and he will find that the difference in favour of the Liberal Conservative government is $1,505,784. In other words, the present government has expended, during the last six years, on immigration more than double what the Liberal-Conservative government expended during the last six years it was in office. But the hon. gentleman selected one year. Well,
I am willing to take any one year. The expenditure on immigration of the Liberal-Conservative party was small.
And the results were very small.

In the hon. gentleman's county, the census return for the past ten years shows a smaller population than they did the previous ten years. I gave a list last session, showing that in all the very best counties of Ontario, the population was less, according to the census of 1901 than it was in 1891. The hon. gentleman seeks to mislead the committee when he attempts to make us believe that the Liberal-Conservative government expended anything like the amount of money on immigration which this government has expended since 1S96.

The hon. the Minister of the Interior will be pleased, no doubt, that his hon. friend from west Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) took up so much of the time of this House. After starting out with the lecture to hon. gentlemen on this side, after telling us that he had listened during four days to the discussion of this question and was very weary and disgusted, he has just taken up an hour and a half of our time going over the same ground again in order to air his views on this subject which he was so tired of. The hon. gentleman referred to the condition of this country previous to 1896, but every one will agree that since then times have been much better in Canada and all over the world. Therefore there can be no particular credit given the policy of the government for the prosperity we are enjoying to-day. In 1896, and for some years previous, there were very hard times in Canada, as was the case throughout the world, but how were the government of that day met by hon. gentlemen opposite on the great question of immigra-ti n. During those years there was very strong necessity for spending large sums on the encouragement of immigration. Did lion, gentlemen opposite support such a policy ? No, they opposed every item ol' expenditure on immigration. I would like to hear from the hon. the Minister of the Interior whether he has ever met any opposition on this side as regards the amount which he desired to expend for the purpose of encouraging immigration. I venture to say that he has not. He has met some criticism on the administration of liis department. His attention has been called to the reports of the American commissioner, showing what a large number of people have come in who are diseased. AVas it not our duty to do this in order that means might be taken to prevent any further influx of sucii people ? In doing this we are advancing the interests of our people. But the hon. gentleman will never find any Conservatives in this House or out of it, taking occasion to run down this country. He will not find any one connected with the Conservative party writing letters to a leading financial paper in England in order to discourage any desirable class of people from coming to this country or to prevent the investment of capital in this country. On the contrary, we have joined with our hon. friends opposite in congratulations over the good times we are now enjoying, which seem to be general throughout the world, and which I hope will long continue. We hope that the administration of this government will be such as will redound to the benefit of the country and our expenditure will be reasonable, and proper immigration will be encouraged. The hon. gentleman speaks of the present condition in Manitoba and the North-west Territories. Everybody knows that for the last few years we have had good crops in

Manitoba and the North-west. And Is it not a fact-Is it not true of the hon. gentleman's own constituency ?-that prior to 1896, many farmers who had bought agricultural implements on credit were not able to pay for those implements owing to the bad crops ? But, with the good crops of the last few years, they have been able to pay these and other debts, and I venture to say that many of these farmers have good bank accounts to-day. Is this due to the policy of this government ? Not at all; it is due to the good crops

Will my hon. friend permit me one remark ? If he will refer to the record of the crop reports, and will take a series of years prior to 1896 and. a series of years succeeding 1896, I venture to say he wifi lind very little difference in the average year.

I simply leave the statement I have made alongside the statement of the hon. gentleman and leave the people of this country to judge which is correct. There is another factor which has helped them greatly. We know that nothing tends more to draw people to a country than the discovery of gold. We know that the British Columbia mines were largely developed by reason of the discovery of gold. And we know perfectly well that capital has been brought in from every country in the world, and hundreds and thousands of people have come in because of the discovery of gold in British Columbia. The hon. gentleman has spoken of tariff and transportation, and has referred to the year 1881 and succeeding years. I wish to point out to him that had that policy of his friends been carried out, we could not possibly have had the present population in the North-west, for they opposed a transportation policy. Notwithstanding their opposition, the Conservative party carried the line of railway through, and as a result of that policy we have the present development of that country.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We would not have had a country at all but for that.
Certainly. I do not wish to take up more of the time of the committee.
Go for him.

It is not necessary. The hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) is here. Perhaps it has been whispered to him what statements the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) has been making.
I believe that one of these gentlemen has one opinion with regard to the Galicians as immigrants, while the other has quite a different opinion. So I leave these hon. gentlemen to settle their differences. For my part I should be glad to see not merely hundreds of thousands but millions of people coming to this country. There is plenty of room for all. I trust a vigorous 216
policy will be pursued for the encouragement of a good class of immigrants. I have no fault to find so far as the amount of money expended is concerned. If the money is properly expended, the expenditure is not too great in the interest of the country. There are points that, I think, could be fairly criticised. I doubt whether it is wise to have so many immigration agents in the United States paid by commission. I do not dwell upon that, because there are other hon. gentlemen who have given the matter more consideration than I have and are more competent to speak upon. it. As a member of the opposition I can say that we are not open to the charge of having, refused our approval to the appropriation of any reasonable sum for immigration purposes.

I think it is somewhat unfortunate that our good friend from West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) has aroused the spirit in this discussion which we observe. Matters were proceeding very nicely, and the estimates of the minister were being discussed in a very temperate manner until our good friend came in and got the blood circulating rather quickly. I hope, however, it will calm down. As to the credit due to the Minister of the Interior, and as to the condemnation of the policy of the Conservative party, a great deal of extravagant language has been used by the hon. member for West Assiniboia. r stand here prepared to prove to any reasonable audience that the reason the Northwest was not colonized to a greater extent up to 1896 was mainly the cause assigned by the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram). It was due to disloyalty of the leaders of the Liberal party, whose speeches were used by the immigration agents of the western and south-western states throughout: the length and breadth of the world to keep colonists out of Canada and induce them to go to the United States.
I suppose that caused the bad crops that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) was speaking about ?

I am not speaking of bad crops. There will be bad crops in the North-west for all time whenever you will find bad farming. And there will be good crops for all time where you And farmers who know how to put in their crops, properly. I say, in all fairness to the Minister of the Interior-and I speak of what I chance to know something about-that he has shown great energy in advertising our North-west in the western states and in the British islands. I do not say that all the money has been judiciously expended. I suppose it will be hard to find any large expenditure, every part of which is quite judicious. I am quite willing to give him the credit he deserves. But I am not willing that any man should stand up in this House and condemn the policy of the Con-



servatives in this regard. And I should think the Liberals would be ashamed to refer to the North-west in connection with immigration; for, as I said, the speeches of the Liberal leaders were used in England, and on the continent of Europe to keep immigrants out of Canada and bring them into the United States. Reference has been made to the Barr colonists. It was my privilege to see a large number of those colonists and on a previous occasion I told the House that I found them to be a very desirable lot of immigrants. And, in this connection, I may say that there is a good deal of fault found by some people with regard to the classes of immigrants. But let it be remembered that the men who raise the straight objection with regard to the importation of mechanics, the importation of labourers, the importation of farm labourers and farmers-these people, not so many years ago, themselves landed on the docks in this country. I want that to be borne in mind. If we are ever to make this country great we must encourage all desirable classes of immigrants. We must keep out the undesirable-especially those physically undesirable, those diseased in mind or body. But, so long as a man has a clear head and an honest heart, I care not if he has not a dollar, let him be brought in and he will find the means of making an honest living. So far as the Barr colonists are concerned, they are a superior lot, and, so far as the colony is concerned, a finer tract of land than that upon which they are settled is not to be found in the Dominion of Canada, or on the continent of North America. What I wish to ask the minister, and I shall be pleased if he will answer me when I am through is, whether there are any large tracts of land set apart in the North-west for Nestorians, Arabians, or any other class not of our own people.
No.
I presume that policy will not be followed any more. I understood that certain lands had been set apart for a number of Poles.
No.

Some gentlemen have" criticised the Doukhobors. I noticed that as soon as the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) came in, the hon. member for West Assiniboia became more docile and assumed a much milder tone than he had previously done. Now, we must admit. of course, that when the tide of immigration is large, a certain number will come in who are ignorant and undesirable. But I do want to say this, that the Galicians have taught the people of Canada to know the value of our poor lands. The hon. member for Alberta knows well that along the south shore of the North Saskatchewan river are regions that no person, even the Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
most enthusiastic and optimistic Canadian, ever imagined were fit for settlement ; yet these people have gone in there among those hills and have shown us that a rolling hill country, which most of us thought to be useless for settlement, can be converted into a prosperous country. The people are now living contented and happy on their own homes ; they are as comfortable and as prosperous, to all appearances, as any that can be found in the older settled parts of Canada.
I would ask the hon. minister if there is any agent in Prince Edward Island to direct persons who want to leave that province to take up their home in the North-west ?
No.

I think it is very desirable that some person should be appointed in that province for that purpose, because there are numbers of our young men who drift away from our island to the United States who, if they were properly directed, would go to western Canada. I think it would be good policy for this government to appoint an agent in Prince Edward Island for the purpose of directing our people who desire to make their homes in the west, and if possible to procure for them a lower fare on the railways than they can now procure. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) told us last night of the great surplus of labour down in the lower provinces. He said it was impossible to find a man to do a day's work, they were all so busily engaged ; that times were good, every person was employed, and the man who desired to procure labour couldn't find it there. Now, the hon. gentleman was certainly drawing on his imagination. We all remember that when men were wanted to reap the harvest in the North-west Territories, and when there was a reduced railway fare, and a chance for our young men in the lower provinces to take a trip to the North-west and to view the country, the trains were overcrowded with those who desired to go out there and work a couple of months for $40 or $50. Now, if they had had employment at home they would not have done that. I am sorry to bring this up before the committee, but the truth must be stated, that twb years ago the trains were overloaded with these young men from the eastern provinces who were seeking employment in the west. We remember that when they found themselves there they were abused, no accommodation was provided for them. One would think that after they had left their homes and travelled thousands of miles to work on the farms, they would have found at least a couple of months' work. I thiuk the government should have done something to assist those young men. Many of our young men drift away to the United States. The Minister of Finance said a few days

ago that there were always some adventurers, some enterprising spirits who would leave the country. Sir, lion, gentlemen opposite have changed their tune. I remember when, in this parliament, blue ruin was preached by the hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce, when we were told that the young men were being driven out of the country by the policy of the late government. There was no talk then of adventurers and enterprising spirits. But if we have now adventurers and enterprising young men who go away to seek homes for themselves, the least the government can do is to assist them in settling in the Northwest. But they will not do that, they would rather spend the money of this country in bringing in Doukhobors and others who are a menace to the welfare of our people. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) has spoken about what was done under the late government. I remember very well, in this parliament, When every effort was made to assist immigration into Canada, when that great Liberal-Conservative party, under the leadership of Sir John A. Macdonald and his able lieutenants, were building that great railway to open up that country and to take in immigrants, knowing that we had in that far west millions of acres of land uncultivated waiting for the settler. Why, Sir, some of the very people who went in there then now occupy seats on the government benches. We were told the other night by the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) that the only thing that was done during the regime of the Liberal-Conservatives was to take in some Jew pedlars, or something of that kind. Let me tell you, Mr. Chairman, that more than Jew pedlars were taken in. There is not an hon. gentleman representing a constituency in the North-west to-day who did not go in there under the regime of the Liberal-Conservatives. The hon. gentleman who addressed us a moment ago went in there in the days of the Liberal-Conservative party. The hon. member for Saskatchewan said he had been there for twenty-two years.
That was before the Conservatives were in power.

The hon. gentleman
himself went in there as an assistant to Nicholas Flood Davin, at Regina, and he knows it.
The hon. gentleman is quite mistaken.

The hon. gentleman
was there when the Conservatives were in power and he is now representing a constituency that should be represented by the honoured dead. These hon. gentlemen talk about what they are doing now and what was done before. It is true that the Liberal-Conservative party opened up the great North-west. It is true that they built, 216J
through their statesmanship and energy, the great railway that now spans the continent from east to west. It is due to their energy that these hon. gentlemen are participating in the blessings and benefits that we have obtained from Providence through the energy of the Liberal-Conservative party. I desire again to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of the Interior to the fact that if we had an agent down in Prince Edward Island, where hundreds of our young men are leaving our shores each year to take up their abodes in the United States, because we are circumscribed in our limits, great good would result. The land is all taken up and is occupied by farmers. When young men grow up they must leave the farm and take up other occupations. If the hon. minister would endeavour to assist these young men, not in the way of paying them any money or anything of that kind, but in the way of obtaining for them during the summer excursion rates over the railway in order that they might go to the North-west, it would be greatly to the advantage of Canada, because one young Canadian from the east or from any part of the country going into the North-west Territories, having a knowledge of farming, and having the experience that is acquired by a young man who lives on a farm, is worth a dozen or two of those Doukhobors that the hon. minister has been paying $20 a head for during the last few years.

I would like to ask the hon. minister if he has any system in his department as to the charge for living expenses, horse-hire, and expenses of that kind. Is it a general principle in his department that employees are allowed to charge up to the country the cost of accident insurance policies ?

The expenses to w-liich the hon. gentleman has been referring simply consists of travelling expenses. Of course, horse-hire is charged up when the official is travelling on public business. In case an official of the department has transportation from the railway companies, as some of them have, and travels on a pass and does not, therefore, charge any railway fare, he has no right to action in case of an accident, and the department pay for the accident insurance. He would have no right of accident against the railway company in case of accident on account of the fact that he is travelling on a pass.

The Department of Marine and Fisheries has a certain schedule of living expenses, and officials such as fishery
inspectors used to make their charges in accordance with that schedule. They must charge so much for horse-hire and no more, and so much for meals and no more. I am

*bound to say, when looking over this item .of horse-hire, that $25 a day for horse-hire is too much. I find a charge here for seven days' horse-hire, $75. There is no place in Canada where a man would require to pay $25 a day for horse-hire. 1 would not mention this gentleman's name if it had not been mentioned before, but I find that Mr. W. W. Cory charged for accident insurance $35. I beg to differ from the hon. minister in regard to that matter. If a man occupies a position under the government at a high salary-I do not care whether he has transportation from the railways or not-he has no light to expect the government to pay for his accident insurance policy. I do not think the government are justified in paying it. Twenty-five dollars a day for horse-nire is far beyond all reason.
How many horses ?

I do not care if there were one or two horses. When we find that this gentleman purchases an eiderdown robe at $25, 1 think he is going a little too far. If the 'country is going to pay for everything like that I think this high toned gentleman should be contented with a little less than these articles, the expenditure on [DOT]which we see detailed in the Auditor General's Report. I would advise the hon. minister to carefully peruse that report and prevent items of this kind being put into it. If the opposition were to do their duty strictly to the letter, they would carefully go through all these items and take up the time of the House in finding fault with them. Surely it is not necessary to do more than simply draw the attention of the minister to some of these items which are extravagant and unreasonable and which, I think, ought not to appear.

The department's attention has been drawn to this matter by the Auditor General. This gentleman did not travel on a pass at all. He has perpetrated what I call a fraud. He did not even buy a return ticket, and the Auditor General drew the attention of the deputy minister to the fact that he had taken $40 or $50 out of the country that he was not entitled to. It is nothing short of a fraud perpetrated upon the country that this official of the government should be able to take out of the pockets of the people that sum of money ? The attention of the department has been drawn to the fact that he not only got his fare, amounting to between $300 and $400, but that lie bought a ticket each way, not a return ticket. The Auditor General drew the attention of the deputy minister to the fact that he might have bought a return ticket and saved $40 or $50.
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR The general principle is that where an Mr. INGRAM.
officer has transportation we pay for his accident insurance policy. In this particular case my deputy tells me that Mr. Cory was charged an excess price f r his accident insurance policy on account of having to travel to the Ydkon in the discharge of his official duties. Under the conditions of the policy he would require to pay an additional amount because he went out of a certain territory.

There are others who have to pay that.
The,' MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR. That is the explanation which is furnished to me. The officer had to hire a team and according to the scale for other things $25 a day would not be out .of the way.

In some departments they fix a limit per day for horse-hire and it seems to work well. With respect to accident insurance there is a rumour in this city that a certain gentleman takes advantage of his position to intimidate government employees in order to get their insurance; that their insurance is dropped in other companies and this man gets the insurance by reason of his position. That is common rumour in Ottawa and if the minister will inquire from the insurance companies he will find that the statement I make is pretty nearly correct.
I could not very well inquire unless I have the name.
I will give the minister the name privately.
Very well.

Why was $8,000 paid to the Rake St. John Railway and Colonization Company ?
The' MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR. This company does a considerable amount of immigration work and this annual grant has been made to them for some years past. The subject was discussed fully the other evening. They made a report showing what they have done.
Where can we see that report.

It is not printed, but I can bring it down if the hon. gentleman desires.
Government of- the North-west Territories, $3,000.
It is perfectly understood of course that all these items can be discussed again.
There is a vote of $250,000 for the Northwest Territories and everything in connection with the matter may be discussed on that.

This vote of $250,000 is an allowance to the North-west government for the year that has expired, and as I fancy there will not be much opposition to it, and as it can be discussed in the supplementary estimates I would like to get the vote passed as it is urgently needed.
It has been arranged that that item should stand.
I do not wish to disturb any arrangement.

I only express the hope that when the minister brings down his votes for the North-west Territories, in addition to the $250,000, he will see that they are given a little extra, because he must know that they require a much larger grant than they have had in the past for roads and bridges.

I may say that we propose to treat them very liberally.
Some resolutions reported.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.
Can the hon. gentleman say what business will be taken up on Monday ?

After private Bills, which is the first order of business, we will take up a number of the Bills on the Order paper, and if we reach Supply, we will continue with the estimates of the Minister of the Interior. Then there are a few items remaining in the supplementary estimates affecting the various departments, and if possible we would like to pass these.
